research-methods.title: Research Methods (Shodh)
research-methods.description: For master's and PhD scholars: from question to design, qualitative and mixed methods, statistics and reproducibility, ethics, integrity, thesis writing and publishing.

courses.title: From Research Question to Research Design
courses.summary: The first year of any master's or PhD project: sharpening a researchable question, reviewing literature systematically, choosing a design that can actually answer it, and sampling and measuring well.
outcomes: Learners can turn a broad interest into a focused, answerable research question using FINER and PICO
Learners can run a reproducible literature search and synthesise rather than summarise
Learners can match questions to experimental, quasi-experimental and observational designs and reason about causality with DAGs
Learners can choose a sampling strategy and justify sample size
Learners can evaluate measurement reliability and validity

story.title: 'I want to study mobile phones and students'

scenes.text: Priyanka joins an MPhil programme in Hyderabad with a passion: 'I want to study mobile phones and students.'
Her supervisor, Prof. Okafor, asks: 'Which students? Which phones use? Which outcome? Compared with what? Over what time?'

After three weeks of rewriting, her question becomes: 'Among first-year undergraduates in Telangana, is night-time smartphone use associated with sleep duration and next-day attention, and does this differ by hostel vs home residence?'
Now it can be answered, measured and finished within two years.

steps.title: From topic to question
steps.body:
A **topic** is an area (phones and students). A **problem** is a gap or tension (rising phone use; unclear effects on sleep). A **research question** is a precise, answerable query. **Hypotheses** are testable predictions derived from theory.

Question types:
- **Descriptive:** what is the prevalence of X?
- **Relational/associational:** is X associated with Y?
- **Causal:** does X cause Y?
- **Explanatory/mechanistic:** how and why does X affect Y?
- **Exploratory/interpretive (often qualitative):** how do people experience X?

The question type dictates design. Causal questions need designs that can rule out alternatives.

steps.title: FINER and PICO checks
steps.body:
**FINER** (Hulley and colleagues, *Designing Clinical Research*): **F**easible (time, money, access, skills), **I**nteresting, **N**ovel, **E**thical, **R**elevant.

**PICO** (clinical/intervention questions): **P**opulation, **I**ntervention/exposure, **C**omparison, **O**utcome (+ **T**ime → PICOT).

Priyanka's question: P = first-year undergraduates in Telangana; I/E = night-time smartphone use; C = low vs high use, hostel vs home; O = sleep duration, attention.

For qualitative work, **SPIDER** (Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research type) is an alternative.

steps.title: Worked rewrite
steps.body:
Weak: 'Does social media affect mental health?'
- Which platforms? Which mental-health outcome? Which age? Effect over what time? Correlation or causation?

Stronger (descriptive–associational): 'Among 13–17-year-olds in urban Maharashtra, what is the association between daily hours on short-video platforms and depressive symptoms (PHQ-A) over 12 months, controlling for baseline symptoms and sleep?'

Stronger (causal): 'Does a 4-week school-based programme reducing evening social-media use improve sleep and depressive symptoms compared with usual curriculum, in a cluster-randomised trial?'

steps.title: Theory and contribution
steps.body:
Good questions sit inside a **conceptual framework**: which constructs, how they relate, and why. State your **contribution**: new population, better design, new mechanism, replication, measurement improvement, or theory test.

Ask: *If I find X, what changes? If I find not-X, what changes?* If neither result would change anything, rethink the question.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Questions too broad for a thesis ("education in India").
- Mixing several questions with different designs into one study.
- Writing causal language ("impact", "effect") for a cross-sectional survey.
- Choosing a question because of available data, then retrofitting theory.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your current research idea as one sentence. Then rewrite it using PICO(T). Then list one result that would surprise you — and why it would matter.

activity.prompt: Classify each research question by type.

items.text: What proportion of PhD scholars in India report symptoms of anxiety?
Is supervisor contact frequency associated with time to thesis submission?
Does a randomised writing-group intervention increase chapters completed per year?
How do first-generation PhD scholars make sense of belonging in their labs?
What is the median stipend delay across 40 universities?
Does switching to a four-day week reduce absenteeism (difference-in-differences)?

quiz.q: In PICO, 'C' stands for:
quiz.why: In PICO, C stands for Comparison, the comparator group or alternative to the intervention. It is not context, control variable or cohort.

quiz.q: Which FINER element concerns access, money and time?
quiz.why: In FINER, Feasible covers access, money and time. Novel, Ethical and Relevant concern new knowledge, ethics and importance.

quiz.q: A cross-sectional survey question should usually avoid the word:
quiz.why: A cross-sectional survey cannot establish cause, so 'impact' wrongly implies causation. Words like prevalence, association and correlate fit the design.

quiz.q: A good test of a question's value is:
options: Both a positive and a null result would change something
quiz.why: A good question is informative either way: both a positive and a null result would change something. Using available data, sounding impressive or having many variables does not make it valuable.

lessons.title: The literature review: systematic, critical, synthetic

story.title: Three hundred PDFs and no idea

scenes.text: Hamid, a first-year PhD scholar in Aligarh, has downloaded 300 PDFs on microfinance and women's empowerment.
He has read 40, remembers 10 and cannot say what the field knows.
His co-supervisor, Dr. Wanjiru, shows him a search protocol, a citation manager and a synthesis matrix.
In six weeks he can state the three main findings, two contradictions and one gap — with every claim traceable.

steps.title: Types of review
steps.body:
- **Narrative review:** expert overview; flexible but prone to selection bias.
- **Scoping review:** maps the extent and nature of literature (PRISMA-ScR guidance).
- **Systematic review:** pre-specified question, protocol (often registered on **PROSPERO** for health topics), comprehensive search, explicit inclusion criteria, quality appraisal, reported with **PRISMA 2020**.
- **Meta-analysis:** statistical pooling of effect sizes from a systematic review.

A thesis literature review is usually narrative but should borrow systematic habits: documented searches and explicit criteria.

steps.title: Building a search, worked
steps.body:
Concepts: microfinance; women; empowerment.
Synonyms: (microfinance OR microcredit OR "self-help group*" OR SHG) AND (women OR female OR gender) AND (empower* OR agency OR "decision-making" OR autonomy).
- Use databases suited to the field (Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, EconLit, PsycINFO, ERIC; Google Scholar for breadth; Shodhganga for Indian theses).
- Record database, date, exact string, filters and hit counts — this makes the search **reproducible**.
- **Citation chasing:** backward (references of key papers) and forward (who cited them).
- Screen titles/abstracts, then full texts, logging reasons for exclusion.

steps.title: From summary to synthesis
steps.body:
Use a **synthesis matrix**: rows = studies; columns = design, sample, measures, findings, limitations. Then write by *theme*, not by paper:
- Weak: 'Smith (2015) found… Jones (2018) found…'
- Strong: 'Randomised evaluations of microcredit across several countries found modest average effects on household income and mixed effects on women's decision-making (e.g., the six-country set of studies summarised by Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman, 2015), whereas observational studies report larger associations, likely reflecting selection.'

Appraise quality: design, risk of bias (e.g., Cochrane RoB 2 for trials), sample size, measurement, conflicts of interest.

steps.title: Tools and habits
steps.body:
- **Citation manager:** Zotero (free), Mendeley or EndNote — store PDFs, notes, tags, and generate references in any style.
- Read strategically: abstract → figures → discussion → methods for key papers.
- Keep a 'claims log': each claim with its source and page.
- Set alerts for new papers on your terms.
- Stop rule: when new searches return mostly known papers (saturation), move to writing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reviewing only what supports your hypothesis (confirmation bias).
- Citing papers you haven't read (secondary citation without saying so).
- Treating all studies as equal regardless of design.
- Ignoring grey literature and non-English or Indian-language sources relevant to the context.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draft a Boolean search string for your topic with at least two synonyms per concept. Run it in two databases and record the hit counts and date.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of a systematic review.
items: Define the question and eligibility criteria (e.g., PICO)
Search multiple databases with documented strings
Screen titles/abstracts, then full texts, recording exclusions
Extract data and appraise risk of bias

quiz.q: PRISMA 2020 is a guideline for:
quiz.why: PRISMA 2020 is the reporting guideline for systematic reviews. It is not for grants, ethics approval or running ANOVAs.

quiz.q: Forward citation chasing means:
options: Finding later papers that cite a key paper
quiz.why: Forward citation chasing means finding later papers that cite a key paper, i.e. who cited it. Reading a paper's references is backward chasing.

quiz.q: A synthesis-style paragraph is organised by:
quiz.why: A synthesis-style paragraph is organised by theme or finding, combining sources around a point. Organising by year, author or journal impact only lists studies.

quiz.q: Registering a review protocol mainly helps to:
quiz.why: Registering a review protocol reduces selective reporting and duplication by making plans transparent in advance. It does not avoid ethics review or speed publication.

story.title: Did the bicycle scheme keep girls in school?

scenes.text: A state gives free bicycles to girls entering Class 9. Enrolment rises. A minister claims credit.
Economist Dr. Rao asks: 'Would enrolment have risen anyway? Did boys' enrolment also rise?'
She compares girls vs boys, before vs after, in that state vs neighbouring states — a difference-in-differences design.
Design, not statistics software, is what lets you say 'caused'.

steps.title: The hierarchy of designs (for causal questions)
steps.body:
- **Randomised controlled trial (RCT):** random assignment balances measured and unmeasured confounders on average. Variants: cluster, stepped-wedge, factorial, crossover.
- **Quasi-experiments:** no random assignment but a credible comparison:
  - **Difference-in-differences** (needs parallel trends)
  - **Regression discontinuity** (assignment by a cut-off, e.g., scholarship at 75% marks)
  - **Instrumental variables** (an instrument affects treatment but affects the outcome only through it)
  - **Interrupted time series**, synthetic control
- **Observational:** cohort (prospective/retrospective), case–control (efficient for rare outcomes; gives odds ratios), cross-sectional (snapshot; weak for causality).

steps.title: Thinking with DAGs
steps.body:
**Directed acyclic graphs** (Pearl; Hernán & Robins) map assumed causal relations.
- **Confounder:** common cause of exposure and outcome (A ← C → Y) → adjust for it.
- **Mediator:** on the causal path (A → M → Y) → don't adjust if you want the total effect.
- **Collider:** common effect (A → K ← Y) → adjusting for it *creates* bias (collider/selection bias).

Example: studying talent and looks among film stars only (selecting on success, a collider) can produce a spurious negative correlation between talent and looks.

Adjustment sets should come from the DAG, not from 'throw everything in the regression'.

steps.title: Worked difference-in-differences
steps.body:
Girls' Class 9 enrolment: before 60%, after 75% (+15). Boys: before 70%, after 76% (+6).
DiD estimate = 15 − 6 = **+9 percentage points** attributable to the scheme — *if* girls' and boys' trends would have been parallel without it.

Check pre-trends over several years before the scheme; run placebo tests (a fake start year); consider other policies that began at the same time.

This mirrors a real line of research: Muralidharan & Prakash (2017) studied Bihar's bicycle programme using a related triple-difference design.

steps.title: Validity
steps.body:
- **Internal validity:** is the causal inference sound within the study? Threats: confounding, selection, attrition, history, maturation, regression to the mean, testing effects, instrumentation.
- **External validity:** does it generalise to other people, places, times?
- **Construct validity:** do measures and manipulations capture the intended constructs?
- **Statistical conclusion validity:** power, appropriate tests, assumptions (Shadish, Cook & Campbell, 2002).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adjusting for mediators or colliders.
- Interpreting a null result from a small RCT as 'no effect'.
- Ignoring differential attrition between arms.
- Using 'controlled for' as if it guaranteed causality in observational data (residual and unmeasured confounding remain).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw a DAG for 'coaching classes → exam rank'. Add family income, prior marks, motivation and 'attending a top college' (an outcome of rank). Which should you adjust for, and which must you not?

activity.prompt: Match each study situation to the best-fitting design.
pairs: A policy starts in one state but not its neighbours
Studying causes of a rare cancer efficiently
Randomising 60 schools to a new curriculum or usual practice
Following 10,000 adults for 20 years to study diet and heart disease
Rainfall shocks used to predict income's effect on child health

quiz.q: Adjusting for a collider:
quiz.why: Adjusting for a collider can introduce bias because it opens a non-causal path between its causes. It is not a removal of bias or a requirement.

quiz.q: Difference-in-differences relies on the assumption of:
quiz.why: Difference-in-differences assumes parallel trends: without treatment, treated and control groups would have moved in parallel. It does not need random assignment or normality.

quiz.q: Case–control studies naturally estimate:
quiz.why: Case–control studies sample on outcome, so they naturally estimate odds ratios, not prevalence, incidence or risk ratios.

quiz.q: Attrition that differs between trial arms threatens:
quiz.why: Attrition that differs between arms makes the groups no longer comparable, threatening internal validity.

story.title: The survey that only reached smartphone owners

scenes.text: A start-up runs an online survey on household water access in rural Rajasthan and finds 'most families have piped water'.
Field researcher Sunita knows many households without smartphones — or piped water — never saw the link.
Her team designs a multi-stage cluster sample: districts → villages → households, using household listings.
They also pilot their water-access questions, because 'access' meant different things to different people.

steps.title: Probability sampling
steps.body:
Every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection → allows inference to the population with quantifiable error.
- **Simple random:** every unit equally likely
- **Systematic:** every k-th unit from a list (beware periodic patterns)
- **Stratified:** sample within strata (state, gender) → precision and guaranteed subgroup sizes
- **Cluster / multi-stage:** sample groups (villages), then units — cheaper, but less precise; account for the **design effect** (DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ, with m = cluster size and ρ = intra-cluster correlation)

Large Indian surveys (e.g., NFHS, PLFS) use multi-stage stratified designs with survey weights.

steps.title: Non-probability sampling
steps.body:
- **Convenience** (whoever is available), **quota**, **purposive** (information-rich cases), **snowball** (hard-to-reach populations)

Appropriate for exploratory and qualitative research or when no sampling frame exists — but statistical generalisation is limited. Be explicit about this limitation and describe the sample thoroughly.

steps.title: Worked sample size
steps.body:
Estimate a proportion within ±5 percentage points (95% confidence), expected p = 0.4:
n₀ = 1.96² × 0.4 × 0.6 / 0.05² ≈ 369.
With clustering (20 households per village, ρ = 0.05): DEFF = 1 + 19 × 0.05 = 1.95 → n ≈ 720.
Inflate for 10% non-response: ≈ 800 households.

For comparisons and effects, use **power analysis** (Course 3).

steps.title: Measurement: reliability and validity
steps.body:
- **Reliability:** consistency — test–retest, inter-rater (Cohen's κ, ICC), internal consistency (Cronbach's α; McDonald's ω is often preferred)
- **Validity:** content, criterion (concurrent, predictive), **construct** (convergent and discriminant; factor structure)
- **Measurement invariance:** does the instrument mean the same across groups (languages, genders)? Test before comparing means.
- **Translation:** forward–backward translation, cognitive interviewing and piloting for Indian languages

A reliable measure can still be invalid (a consistently wrong scale).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a convenience sample and generalising to 'Indian youth'.
- Ignoring clustering in analysis — standard errors become too small.
- Treating α > 0.7 as proof of validity.
- Comparing groups on a scale that lacks measurement invariance.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick a construct in your field (e.g., 'financial literacy'). List two existing instruments, their reliability evidence, and whether they've been validated in your population and language.

activity.prompt: Cluster sample: 25 households per village, intra-cluster correlation 0.04. What is the design effect (DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ)?

quiz.q: Stratified sampling mainly improves:
quiz.why: Stratified sampling samples within strata, which improves precision and subgroup representation. It is not mainly about cost, response rate or instrument validity.

quiz.q: Snowball sampling is useful for:
quiz.why: Snowball sampling uses referral chains, so it is useful for hard-to-reach populations. It is not suited to national prevalence estimates, randomised trials or a census.

quiz.q: A design effect of 2 means:
options: You need about twice the simple-random sample size
quiz.why: A design effect of 2 means variance is inflated twofold, so you need about twice the simple-random sample size for the same precision.

quiz.q: Measurement invariance should be tested before:
quiz.why: Test measurement invariance before comparing groups' scores, to confirm the instrument measures the same construct across groups. Otherwise differences may reflect measurement, not real differences.

questions.q: FINER's 'E' stands for:
questions.why: In FINER, E stands for Ethical, alongside Feasible, Interesting, Novel and Relevant.

questions.q: A systematic review differs from a narrative review mainly by:
questions.why: A systematic review uses pre-specified, documented, reproducible methods, unlike a narrative review. It is not defined by length or by using only RCTs.

questions.q: Random assignment primarily protects:
questions.why: Random assignment balances confounders across groups, which protects internal validity. It does not by itself ensure reliability or external validity.

questions.q: Which is a probability sampling method?
questions.why: Stratified random sampling is a probability method because each unit has a known selection probability. Quota, convenience and snowball sampling are non-probability.

questions.q: A mediator should be adjusted for when estimating:
questions.why: Adjusting for a mediator is done to estimate the direct effect, with care. For the total effect, you should not adjust for it.

questions.q: Regression discontinuity identifies effects:
questions.why: Regression discontinuity identifies a local effect near the cut-off, not for everyone. It is not limited to RCTs and still needs assumptions.

questions.q: Cohen's κ measures:
questions.why: Cohen's kappa measures inter-rater agreement beyond chance. Validity, internal consistency and test–retest are different properties.

questions.q: A search string combining synonyms within a concept uses:
questions.why: Use OR to combine synonyms within a concept, which widens the search. AND links different concepts and narrows it.

questions.q: Selecting only hospitalised patients to study two diseases can create a spurious association because hospitalisation is a:
questions.why: Selecting only hospitalised patients conditions on hospitalisation, a collider affected by both diseases, which creates a spurious association (Berkson's bias). It is not a confounder, mediator or instrument.

questions.q: Expected p = 0.5, margin ±4%, 95% CI: n₀ ≈
A valid instrument must affect the outcome:
options: Not at all, even through treatment
questions.why: A valid instrument must affect the outcome only through the treatment, which is the exclusion restriction. A direct effect would invalidate it.

questions.q: Pre-trend tests in DiD can:
options: Provide evidence consistent (or not) with parallel trends
questions.why: Pre-trend tests can give evidence consistent or not with parallel trends, but they cannot prove it. They do not replace controls or eliminate confounding.

questions.q: Ignoring clustering in a cluster sample typically leads to:
options: Too-small standard errors and false positives
questions.why: Ignoring clustering underestimates variance, so standard errors are too small and false positives rise. It does not make CIs wider or SEs unbiased.

courses.title: Qualitative and Mixed-Methods Research
courses.summary: How to design, collect, analyse and defend qualitative research — interviews, ethnography, grounded theory, thematic analysis — and how to integrate it with quantitative data in mixed-methods designs.
outcomes: Learners can choose among phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, case study and narrative approaches
Learners can design interview guides and conduct ethical, high-quality interviews and focus groups
Learners can code data and carry out reflexive thematic analysis
Learners can demonstrate rigour using trustworthiness criteria and reflexivity
Learners can design convergent, explanatory and exploratory mixed-methods studies

scenes.text: Public-health researcher Dr. Meenakshi wants to know why some ASHA (community health) workers in Odisha stay for a decade despite low pay.
A survey can tell her how many stay and correlates of staying. It cannot tell her what the work *means* to them.
She spends months interviewing ASHAs, observing village health days and reading their registers.
Themes of respect, identity and 'being needed' emerge — insights no questionnaire had asked about.

steps.title: Paradigms
steps.body:
Research rests on assumptions about reality (**ontology**) and knowledge (**epistemology**):
- **Positivism / post-positivism:** an external reality we can approximate through measurement; aims at explanation and generalisation.
- **Interpretivism / constructivism:** realities are socially constructed; aims at understanding meanings.
- **Critical** approaches (feminist, critical race, Dalit studies): research to expose and challenge power.
- **Pragmatism:** choose methods by what works for the question — common in mixed methods.

You don't need to pledge lifelong allegiance, but your design, sampling and quality criteria should be consistent with your stance.

steps.title: Five common qualitative approaches
steps.body:
- **Phenomenology** (Husserl; interpretative phenomenological analysis — Smith): the lived experience of a phenomenon; small, homogeneous samples; deep interviews.
- **Grounded theory** (Glaser & Strauss, 1967; Charmaz's constructivist version): build theory from data through constant comparison, theoretical sampling and memoing.
- **Ethnography:** immersion in a culture or setting; participant observation, field notes, long engagement.
- **Case study** (Yin; Stake): in-depth study of a bounded system (an organisation, programme, event) using multiple data sources.
- **Narrative inquiry:** stories people tell about their lives and how they're told.

steps.title: Matching question to approach
steps.body:
- 'What is it like to be a first-generation PhD scholar?' → phenomenology
- 'How do ASHAs develop a professional identity over time?' → grounded theory
- 'How is hierarchy enacted in a hospital ward?' → ethnography
- 'How did one district implement a nutrition programme so differently from its neighbour?' → case study
- 'How do Partition survivors narrate displacement?' → narrative inquiry

steps.title: Sampling in qualitative research
steps.body:
Sampling is **purposive**: chosen for information richness.
- Maximum variation, homogeneous, typical, extreme/deviant, critical case, **theoretical** (grounded theory — sample to develop emerging concepts)
- Sample size: guided by **information power** (Malterud et al., 2016) — aim, specificity, theory, dialogue quality, analysis strategy — or by **saturation** (no new codes/themes), though 'saturation' is debated and should be defined, not just claimed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating qualitative research as 'anecdotes' or as a pilot for 'real' research.
- Claiming statistical generalisation from 15 interviews.
- Mixing incompatible quality criteria (e.g., demanding inter-rater reliability for reflexive thematic analysis).
- Not specifying the approach at all ('a qualitative study was done').

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your research question two ways: once as a 'how many / how strongly' quantitative question and once as a 'how / what is it like' qualitative question. Which better serves your aim?

activity.prompt: Match each approach to its signature feature.
pairs: Theory built through constant comparison and theoretical sampling
Bounded system studied with multiple data sources
Stories and how they are told

quiz.q: Pragmatism as a paradigm emphasises:
options: Choosing methods by what best answers the question
quiz.why: Pragmatism chooses methods by what best answers the research question. It does not insist on one true method or only numbers or only meanings.

quiz.q: Theoretical sampling is characteristic of:
quiz.why: Theoretical sampling, where emerging concepts guide whom to sample next, is characteristic of grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss). It is not typical of RCTs or surveys.

quiz.q: Information power (Malterud et al.) is a way to:
quiz.why: Information power (Malterud et al.) is a way to justify qualitative sample size, based on how much the sample can tell you. It is not for reliability, p-values or survey weights.

quiz.q: Generalisation in qualitative research is usually:
quiz.why: Qualitative generalisation is usually analytical, theoretical or based on transferability, not statistical. It is not impossible nor required to be national.

lessons.title: Collecting qualitative data: interviews, focus groups, observation

scenes.text: Rahul, an MA student in Kolkata, interviews gig-economy delivery riders. His first interview lasts 12 minutes.
He asked closed questions: 'Do you like the job? Is pay fair?' The rider answered 'yes', 'no', 'okay'.
His supervisor helps him rewrite: 'Tell me about a typical day, from the moment you wake up.'
The next interview lasts 70 minutes, full of detail about apps, ratings, rain and dignity.

steps.title: Interviews
steps.body:
- **Structured** (fixed questions), **semi-structured** (guide with flexibility — most common), **unstructured** (conversational).
- Good questions are **open**, **non-leading** and **concrete**: 'Tell me about…', 'Walk me through…', 'Can you give an example?'
- Use **probes**: 'What happened next?', 'How did that feel?', 'What do you mean by…?'
- Order: easy, descriptive questions first; sensitive ones later; close with 'Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?'
- **Pilot** the guide; record (with consent) and transcribe; keep field notes about context and non-verbal cues.

steps.title: Focus groups and observation
steps.body:
**Focus groups** (6–10 people): useful for shared norms and how people talk about a topic; group dynamics can silence some voices and are less suited to very sensitive personal topics. A moderator manages turn-taking.

**Participant observation:** spectrum from complete observer to complete participant. Write **thick description** (Geertz) in field notes: what was seen, heard, the setting, and your own reactions (kept separately).

steps.title: Worked: rewriting a guide
steps.body:
Leading: 'Don't you think the app's rating system is unfair?'
Open: 'How do ratings figure in your work?' → probe: 'Can you tell me about a time a rating affected you?'

Double-barrelled: 'How do you feel about your pay and hours?'
Split: 'Tell me about how your earnings work.' / 'What do your working hours look like?'

Jargon: 'How does algorithmic management affect your autonomy?'
Plain: 'How much can you decide for yourself during a shift?'

steps.title: Language, power and positionality
steps.body:
- Interview in participants' preferred language; transcribe and translate carefully, noting terms that resist translation.
- Your caste, gender, class, age, institutional status and accent shape what people tell you. Reflect on this **positionality** and how it might affect access and rapport.
- Compensation should acknowledge time without being coercive.
- Distress protocols: know when to pause and where to refer (e.g., Tele-MANAS 14416 in India).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Talking more than the participant.
- Interrupting silences — pauses often precede the richest answers.
- Promising anonymity you can't guarantee (small communities can identify people from details).
- Transcribing selectively.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draft five open questions for a 45-minute interview on your topic, each with two probes. Pilot one with a friend and note where they hesitated or misunderstood.

statements.s: 'Don't you agree the policy failed?' is a good open question.
statements.why: It is leading and invites agreement.

statements.s: Semi-structured interviews combine a guide with flexibility to follow up.
statements.why: That's their defining feature.

statements.s: Focus groups are ideal for every highly sensitive personal topic.
statements.why: Group settings can inhibit disclosure; individual interviews may be better.

statements.s: Researcher positionality can shape what participants share.
statements.why: Power, identity and status affect interactions.

statements.s: Silences in interviews should be filled immediately.
statements.why: Waiting often yields deeper answers.

quiz.q: Which is an effective probe?
quiz.why: 'Can you give me an example?' is an effective probe because it elicits detail. Leading or closed prompts like 'Right?' do not.

quiz.q: Thick description is associated with:
quiz.why: Thick description is associated with Clifford Geertz, who stressed rich context and meaning. Fisher, Likert and Yin are linked to other ideas.

quiz.q: A double-barrelled question:
quiz.why: A double-barrelled question asks two things at once, so the answer is ambiguous; split it into two questions.

quiz.q: Before main data collection you should:
quiz.why: Pilot the interview guide before main data collection, because piloting refines questions. Skipping it risks flawed questions.

scenes.text: Dr. Meenakshi now has 38 ASHA interview transcripts — around 2,000 pages in Odia and English.
She codes line by line, noting 'being called didi', 'carrying the register at night', 'doctor's respect'.
Codes cluster into candidate themes; some merge, some split, one disappears when she rereads the data.
Her final themes tell a story about identity and recognition, backed by quotes and her analytic commentary.

steps.title: Coding
steps.body:
A **code** labels a meaningful segment of data.
- **Inductive** (data-driven) vs **deductive** (theory-driven) coding — many studies combine both.
- **Semantic** (explicit content) vs **latent** (underlying ideas and assumptions).
- Keep a **codebook** (name, definition, example, when not to use) and analytic **memos** recording your thinking.
- Software such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA or the free QualCoder/Taguette helps organise — it doesn't analyse for you.

steps.title: Reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke)
steps.body:
Six phases (2006; refined as 'reflexive TA', 2019/2021):
1. Familiarise yourself with the data
2. Generate initial codes
3. Construct candidate themes
4. Review themes against coded data and the whole dataset
5. Define and name themes
6. Write up

A **theme** is a pattern of shared meaning organised around a central concept — not just a topic summary ('Participants discussed pay') but an interpretive claim ('Pay was framed as secondary to recognition, yet its lateness was read as disrespect'). Braun & Clarke argue inter-coder reliability scores are inconsistent with reflexive TA's interpretive logic; codebook and coding-reliability approaches differ.

steps.title: Other analytic approaches
steps.body:
- **Grounded theory:** open → focused/axial → theoretical coding; constant comparison; theoretical memos; aim: a substantive theory
- **IPA:** idiographic case-by-case analysis, then cross-case themes
- **Framework analysis** (Ritchie & Spencer): matrix-based, good for policy research and teams
- **Discourse and conversation analysis:** how language constructs reality or organises interaction
- **Content analysis:** can be quantitative (counting) or qualitative

steps.title: Writing up a theme
steps.body:
Theme: **'Being needed at night'**
- Analytic claim: ASHAs' sense of worth crystallised in night-time emergencies, when they accompanied women in labour to the facility.
- Evidence: 2–3 well-chosen quotes from different participants (with pseudonyms and relevant context, e.g., 'ASHA, 9 years').
- Interpretation: how this links to identity, recognition and retention; connections to literature on care work.
- Variation: participants for whom night duty was a source of fear, not pride.

Quotes illustrate; your analysis argues.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using interview questions as themes.
- Presenting themes as 'emerging' on their own — the researcher actively constructs them.
- Only quoting articulate participants.
- Counting mentions as if frequency equalled importance.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take one page of a transcript (or an interview you find online with permission for reuse). Code it with 8–10 codes. Group them into two candidate themes and write a one-sentence central concept for each.

activity.prompt: Order Braun & Clarke's phases of reflexive thematic analysis.

quiz.q: A theme in reflexive TA is best described as:
options: A pattern of shared meaning around a central concept
quiz.why: In reflexive thematic analysis, a theme is a pattern of shared meaning organised around a central concept. It is not just a topic heading, a frequency count or a question.

quiz.q: Latent coding focuses on:
quiz.why: Latent coding looks at underlying ideas and assumptions beneath the surface. Semantic coding looks at explicit words.

quiz.q: Framework analysis is particularly suited to:
options: Applied policy research with teams and matrices
quiz.why: Framework analysis (Ritchie and Spencer) suits applied policy research with teams, using matrices. It is not for lab experiments or meta-analysis.

quiz.q: Qualitative analysis software:
quiz.why: Qualitative software helps organise coding and retrieval; it does not analyse data automatically or replace the researcher. It is not required for validity.

story.title: The reviewer who asked for p-values

scenes.text: Meenakshi submits her paper. Reviewer 2 asks, 'How many participants mentioned respect? Is it statistically significant?'
She replies by explaining her paradigm and demonstrating trustworthiness: reflexive memos, thick description, negative cases and member reflections.
For a follow-up grant, she designs a mixed-methods study: a state-wide survey of retention, then interviews to explain surprising survey patterns.
Numbers and narratives, each doing what it does best.

steps.title: Trustworthiness (Lincoln & Guba, 1985)
steps.body:
Parallel criteria for qualitative rigour:
- **Credibility** (≈ internal validity): prolonged engagement, triangulation, negative case analysis, peer debriefing, member checking/reflections
- **Transferability** (≈ external validity): thick description so readers can judge fit to their context
- **Dependability** (≈ reliability): audit trail of decisions
- **Confirmability** (≈ objectivity): findings traceable to data; reflexivity

Other frameworks: Tracy's 'eight big-tent criteria' (2010). Reporting checklists: **COREQ** (for interviews/focus groups) and **SRQR**.

steps.title: Reflexivity
steps.body: Keep a reflexive journal: your assumptions before starting, reactions during fieldwork, and how your identity and choices shaped the data and interpretation. In write-ups, include a short **positionality statement** where appropriate — specific and relevant, not a list of identity labels.

steps.title: Mixed-methods designs (Creswell & Plano Clark)
steps.body:
- **Convergent:** collect quant and qual in parallel, analyse separately, then compare/merge (joint displays)
- **Explanatory sequential:** quant first, then qual to explain results (Meenakshi's follow-up)
- **Exploratory sequential:** qual first to explore, then build and test an instrument or hypotheses quantitatively
- Embedded/intervention designs: qualitative process evaluation within a trial

The key is **integration** — at design, methods (sampling, data collection) and interpretation stages. Otherwise you have two studies stapled together.

steps.title: Worked joint display
steps.body:
Survey: ASHAs reporting supervisor support were 1.8× more likely to stay (illustrative).
Interviews: 'support' meant timely payments and being defended in front of doctors, not training.
Joint display row: Domain = support | Quant = higher retention | Qual = respect + payment timeliness | Meta-inference = 'support' operates through recognition; measure it differently next time.

Divergence is valuable: it reveals construct or measurement problems.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using member checking as proof that interpretations are 'correct' — participants may disagree with legitimate analytic interpretations.
- Calling any study with an open-ended survey question 'mixed methods'.
- No integration plan.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Sketch a mixed-methods design for your topic: name the design type, the order of strands, the point(s) of integration, and one way findings could diverge.

a.text: A reviewer writes: 'With only 20 interviews, the findings are not generalisable and the coding lacks inter-rater reliability.' How do you respond?

choices.label: Apologise and add a chi-square test of theme frequencies
choices.feedback: That applies quantitative logic inconsistently with your design.

choices.label: Explain the paradigm and analytic approach, and show how trustworthiness was ensured

b.text: Your co-author worries the test misrepresents your reflexive TA. What now?

choices.label: Remove it and instead explain information power, thick description and the audit trail
Keep it; reviewers like numbers

c.text: The reviewer also asks how your identity may have shaped interviews with ASHAs. What do you add?

choices.label: A concise positionality and reflexivity section describing specific influences and how you handled them
A statement that you were completely objective
choices.feedback: Qualitative rigour acknowledges, rather than denies, the researcher's role.

end1.text: The paper is accepted after minor revisions; the reviewer thanks you for a clear methodological rationale.

end2.text: The editor flags methodological inconsistency. Revisit trustworthiness criteria and how to defend qualitative designs.

quiz.q: 'Transferability' is supported mainly by:
quiz.why: Transferability is supported mainly by thick description, so readers can judge whether findings fit their context. Kappa, large samples and p-values are not the route.

quiz.q: COREQ is a checklist for reporting:
quiz.why: COREQ is the checklist for reporting qualitative interview and focus-group studies. RCTs, systematic reviews and diagnostic studies have other guidelines.

quiz.q: An explanatory sequential design starts with:
quiz.why: An explanatory sequential design starts with quantitative data and then uses qualitative work to explain it.

quiz.q: The hallmark of genuine mixed methods is:
quiz.why: The hallmark of genuine mixed methods is integration of the strands. Having two datasets, large samples or software is not enough.

questions.q: Ontology concerns:
questions.why: Ontology concerns the nature of reality. Sampling, ethics forms and data cleaning are practical matters.

questions.q: Grounded theory was introduced by:
questions.why: Grounded theory was introduced by Glaser and Strauss in 1967. Braun and Clarke are linked to thematic analysis.

questions.q: Purposive sampling selects participants for:
questions.why: Purposive sampling selects participants for information richness, i.e. cases that can give rich data. It is not random or about statistical power.

questions.q: Which is an open interview question?
options: Is pay fair, yes or no?
Tell me about a typical working day.
questions.why: 'Tell me about a typical working day' is open and invites narrative. Yes/no and leading questions limit answers.

questions.q: Member checking contributes to:
questions.why: Member checking contributes to credibility, by letting participants confirm interpretations (Lincoln and Guba). It is not about blinding or power.

questions.q: IPA is:
options: Idiographic, focusing on lived experience case by case
questions.why: IPA, interpretative phenomenological analysis, is idiographic: it examines lived experience case by case. It is not a survey method or meta-analysis.

questions.q: An audit trail supports:
questions.why: An audit trail makes decisions traceable, which supports dependability. It does not give power, randomisation or transferability.

questions.q: An exploratory sequential design is suitable when:
options: You need to explain survey outliers
Instruments don't exist for the population and must be developed
questions.why: An exploratory sequential design suits cases where instruments do not exist for the population and must be developed, with qualitative work informing the quantitative phase.

questions.q: Braun & Clarke argue inter-coder reliability is:
options: Inconsistent with reflexive TA's interpretive logic
questions.why: Braun and Clarke argue that inter-coder reliability is inconsistent with reflexive TA's interpretive logic, where the researcher's subjectivity is a resource. It is not essential there.

questions.q: Negative case analysis means:
options: Actively examining cases that don't fit emerging patterns
questions.why: Negative case analysis means actively examining cases that do not fit emerging patterns, which strengthens credibility. It does not mean deleting data.

questions.q: A joint display is used to:
options: Integrate quantitative and qualitative findings side by side
questions.why: A joint display integrates quantitative and qualitative findings side by side. It is not an ethics report or transcripts display.

questions.q: A key critique of 'data saturation' as a sample-size justification is that it is:
options: Often claimed without definition and fits poorly with interpretive approaches
questions.why: 'Data saturation' is often claimed without definition and fits poorly with interpretive approaches (Braun and Clarke; Malterud). It is not too mathematical or illegal.

questions.q: Thick description is mainly a strategy for:
questions.why: Thick description mainly supports transferability by giving contextual detail so readers can judge fit. It is not a strategy for reliability or power.

courses.title: Statistics and Reproducibility for Researchers
courses.summary: The statistical decisions that make or break a thesis — power and effect sizes, choosing and checking models, avoiding questionable research practices, preregistration, and a fully reproducible workflow.
outcomes: Learners can plan sample size with a priori power analysis and a justified smallest effect size of interest
Learners can report effect sizes and confidence intervals and interpret them substantively
Learners can choose appropriate models (GLMs, mixed models) and check assumptions
Learners can recognise and prevent p-hacking, HARKing and garden-of-forking-paths problems
Learners can build a reproducible workflow with scripts, version control, data management and open materials

lessons.title: Effect sizes, power and sample size

scenes.text: Vikram, a PhD scholar in Bengaluru, ran an experiment with 12 participants per group. The result: p = 0.21. 'My intervention doesn't work,' he says.
His committee member, Dr. Lindqvist, asks, 'What effect size could you detect with 80% power?' The answer: about d = 1.2 — a huge effect.
Vikram's study could only have found a gigantic effect. A null result tells him almost nothing.
Next time he plans power *before* collecting data.

steps.title: Effect sizes
steps.body:
- **Standardised mean difference** (Cohen's d, Hedges' g for small-sample correction): difference / pooled SD
- **Correlation r**, **R²**, **η²/ω²** (variance explained)
- **Odds ratio, risk ratio, risk difference** for binary outcomes; **number needed to treat** = 1/risk difference

Cohen's benchmarks (d = 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) were offered as a last resort; interpret effects in **context** (cost, scale, outcome importance). Many well-replicated effects in psychology and education are small (d ≈ 0.1–0.3).

steps.title: Power
steps.body:
**Power** = P(reject H₀ | true effect = δ). Depends on α, n, effect size and design (paired, within-subject and covariate-adjusted designs increase power).

Why low power is harmful (Button et al., 2013; median power in neuroscience studies they examined was about 21%):
- Many true effects are missed
- Significant results are more likely false positives (lower positive predictive value)
- Significant estimates are inflated (**winner's curse** / Type M error; Gelman & Carlin's Type S and Type M errors)

steps.title: Worked power analysis
steps.body:
Two-group comparison, two-sided α = 0.05, power 0.80.
Approximate n per group ≈ 2 × (z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)² / d² = 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² / d² ≈ 15.7 / d².
- d = 0.5 → ≈ 63 per group (exact t-test calculation: 64)
- d = 0.3 → ≈ 175 per group
- d = 0.2 → ≈ 393 per group

Vikram's n = 12 per group: d detectable at 80% ≈ √(15.7/12) ≈ 1.14 (exact t-test ≈ 1.2).

Tools: G*Power (free), R packages (pwr, simr for mixed models), or **simulation** for complex designs.

steps.title: Justifying the effect size
steps.body:
Don't power for the effect in a single small published study (likely inflated). Options (Lakens, 2022, 'Sample size justification'):
- **Smallest effect size of interest (SESOI):** the smallest effect that would matter practically or theoretically
- Meta-analytic estimates corrected for bias
- Resource constraints, honestly stated, with the detectable effect reported

For nulls, use **equivalence testing** (TOST) against the SESOI or Bayes factors to argue for absence of a meaningful effect.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Post-hoc power' computed from the observed effect — it is a transformation of the p-value and adds no information.
- Treating p > 0.05 as evidence of no effect.
- Reporting only p-values without effect sizes and CIs.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Decide a SESOI for your main outcome in real units (e.g., 3 marks on a 100-mark test, 15 minutes of sleep). Convert it to d using a plausible SD, then compute n per group with the formula above.

activity.label: True standardised effect size (Cohen's d) for a two-group study, n = 50 per group, α = 0.05

bands.text: Power is roughly 5–15%: you will almost always miss this effect, and any significant result will greatly overestimate it.
Power roughly 15–45%: a coin-flip at best. Typical of many small published studies; expect inflated significant estimates.
Power roughly 45–80%: improving, but still below the conventional 80% for d below ~0.57.
Power roughly 80–98%: well powered for this effect.
Power near 100%: only plausible if the effect is truly this large — rare in behavioural and social science.

quiz.q: n per group for d = 0.5, 80% power, α = 0.05 (two-sided t-test) is about:
quiz.why: For d = 0.5, 80% power and α = 0.05 (two-sided t-test), n ≈ 2(1.96+0.84)²/d² = 15.7/0.25 ≈ 64 per group.

quiz.q: Low power increases the chance that a significant result:
quiz.why: Low power raises the chance that a significant result overestimates the true effect (the winner's curse), because only large estimates cross the threshold.

quiz.q: Post-hoc 'observed power' is problematic because it:
options: Is a direct function of the observed p-value
quiz.why: Post-hoc observed power is a direct function of the observed p-value, so it adds no information. It is not fixed at 80%.

quiz.q: To argue that an effect is negligibly small, use:
quiz.why: To argue an effect is negligibly small, use equivalence testing (TOST) against a smallest effect size of interest. A non-significant t-test cannot show absence of an effect.

scenes.text: Sana's dataset: 4,000 students in 80 schools across Uttar Pradesh, with test scores and a school-level intervention.
A plain regression gives p < 0.001. Her advisor frowns: 'You've treated 4,000 students as independent. They aren't — they share schools.'
A multilevel model with school random intercepts gives a wider CI and p = 0.04.
The model must match how the data were generated.

steps.title: The generalised linear model family
steps.body:
- **Linear regression:** continuous outcome, normal residuals
- **Logistic regression:** binary outcome; coefficients are log-odds (exponentiate for odds ratios)
- **Poisson / negative binomial:** counts (negative binomial when overdispersed)
- **Ordinal (proportional odds):** Likert-type ordered outcomes
- **Survival models** (Cox): time-to-event with censoring

ANOVA and t-tests are special cases of the linear model.

steps.title: Dependence: multilevel/mixed models
steps.body:
When observations are clustered (students in schools, repeated measures in people, items in participants), use **mixed-effects models** with random intercepts (and random slopes where justified).
- The **intraclass correlation (ICC)** says how much variance is between clusters.
- Treatment varying at the school level? Your effective sample size is closer to the number of schools than students.
- In experimental psychology, treat both participants and **stimuli** as random factors where stimuli are sampled (Judd, Westfall & Kenny, 2012).

Alternatives: cluster-robust standard errors, GEE (population-averaged effects).

steps.title: Checking assumptions
steps.body:
- **Residual plots:** linearity, constant variance (heteroscedasticity → robust SEs or transformation)
- **Normality of residuals** (not of raw variables) — matters mainly for small samples and prediction intervals
- **Influential points:** Cook's distance, leverage
- **Multicollinearity:** variance inflation factors
- **Overdispersion** for counts
- **Missing data:** distinguish MCAR, MAR, MNAR; prefer **multiple imputation** or full-information maximum likelihood over listwise deletion when data are MAR

steps.title: Worked interpretation
steps.body:
Logistic model for passing (1/0): log-odds = −1.2 + 0.35 × hours_tutoring.
Odds ratio = e^0.35 ≈ **1.42** → each extra hour multiplies the odds of passing by 1.42 (a 42% increase in *odds*, not probability).
At 0 hours: p = 1/(1 + e^1.2) ≈ 0.23; at 4 hours: log-odds = 0.2 → p ≈ 0.55.

Report predicted probabilities at meaningful values; odds ratios are often misread as risk ratios.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring clustering (Sana's first model).
- Treating a 5-point Likert item as continuous without checking whether conclusions change with an ordinal model.
- Dichotomising continuous variables (median splits) — loses power and can create spurious effects.
- Stepwise selection followed by standard inference — p-values are no longer valid.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write the model formula for your main analysis (e.g., score ~ treatment + baseline + (1 | school)). Next to each term, write why it's there — from your DAG or design, not from p-values.

activity.prompt: Match each outcome/data structure to the most appropriate model.
pairs: Number of hospital visits, variance ≫ mean
Time until dropout, some still enrolled
Repeated weekly mood ratings per person
Mixed-effects model with person random effects

quiz.q: An odds ratio of 1.42 means:
quiz.why: An odds ratio of 1.42 means the odds multiply by 1.42. It is not the same as risk doubling or a 42-point rise in probability.

quiz.q: Ignoring clustering usually makes standard errors:
quiz.why: Ignoring clustering overstates precision, so standard errors are too small and false positives rise.

quiz.q: Which assumption concerns residuals, not raw variables?
quiz.why: Normality in linear models concerns the residuals, not the raw variables. Sample size, ethics and randomisation are not residual assumptions.

quiz.q: When data are missing at random (MAR), a generally preferred approach is:
quiz.why: When data are missing at random, multiple imputation is generally preferred because it is valid under MAR and keeps uncertainty. Listwise deletion and mean imputation can bias or understate variance.

lessons.title: Questionable research practices and how to prevent them

scenes.text: Late at night, Neha tries her analysis with and without outliers, with three different covariates, and with two of four outcome measures.
Version 7 gives p = 0.03. She feels relief — and unease.
She reads Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2011): flexible analysis choices can push false-positive rates far above 5%.
She writes a preregistration for her next study before seeing any data.

steps.title: What QRPs are
steps.body:
Practices that inflate false positives while falling short of outright fraud:
- **p-hacking:** trying analyses until p < 0.05 (optional stopping, dropping conditions, choosing outcomes or covariates post hoc, outlier rules decided after seeing results)
- **HARKing** (Kerr, 1998): Hypothesising After the Results are Known, presented as if a priori
- **Selective reporting** of studies, outcomes or analyses (the 'file drawer')
- **Rounding down** p-values (e.g., 0.054 reported as 'p < 0.05')

John, Loewenstein & Prelec (2012) surveyed psychologists and found that many admitted to at least one such practice. Simmons et al. (2011) showed combining a few flexible choices can raise false-positive rates to about 60%.

steps.title: The garden of forking paths
steps.body:
Gelman & Loken: even without consciously 'fishing', data-dependent analysis choices create multiple potential comparisons. The p-value assumes one pre-specified analysis.

**Multiverse analysis** (Steegen et al., 2016) and **specification curve analysis** (Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson) report results across all reasonable analytic choices to show robustness.

steps.title: Preregistration and Registered Reports
steps.body:
- **Preregistration:** a time-stamped plan (hypotheses, design, sample size and stopping rule, exclusions, primary analysis) on OSF Registries, AsPredicted or trial registries (CTRI in India for clinical trials; ClinicalTrials.gov).
- Deviations are allowed but must be **reported transparently**; exploratory analyses are welcome when labelled as such.
- **Registered Reports** (Chambers; introduced at *Cortex* in 2013): journals peer-review the introduction and methods *before* data collection and grant in-principle acceptance regardless of results. Scheel, Schijen & Lakens (2021) found about 44% positive results in Registered Reports vs about 96% in standard psychology reports they sampled.

steps.title: Worked preregistration snippet
steps.body:
H1: Students receiving spaced-retrieval homework will score higher on the end-of-term test than controls.
- Design: cluster RCT, 40 classrooms
- Sample size: 40 classrooms × ~30 students, giving 80% power for d = 0.25 given ICC = 0.15 (simulation code attached)
- Exclusions: students absent for the final test (reported by arm)
- Primary analysis: mixed model score ~ arm + baseline + (1 | classroom); two-sided α = 0.05
- Secondary/exploratory: effects by baseline achievement tercile (labelled exploratory)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Preregistering vaguely ('we will analyse the data appropriately').
- Hiding deviations from the preregistration.
- Thinking preregistration forbids exploration — it only requires honest labelling.
- Correcting for multiple comparisons inconsistently (choose a strategy in advance: Bonferroni/Holm for familywise error; Benjamini–Hochberg for false discovery rate).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a five-line preregistration for your next study: hypothesis, primary outcome, sample size justification, exclusion rule, primary model.

a.text: Your preregistered primary outcome shows p = 0.11. A secondary outcome shows p = 0.02. Your co-author suggests making the secondary outcome 'the main result'. What do you do?

choices.label: Switch the outcomes and rewrite the introduction
Report the primary result as preregistered, with effect size and CI; report the secondary as secondary

b.text: A reviewer compares your paper with the preregistration and spots the switch. What now?

choices.label: Acknowledge it, restore the preregistered primary analysis, and label the rest as secondary/exploratory
choices.feedback: Correcting the record is the right step.

choices.label: Argue that preregistrations don't matter
choices.feedback: This damages credibility and may lead to rejection.

c.text: How do you discuss the null primary result?

choices.label: Interpret the CI relative to the SESOI and discuss what effects remain plausible
Say 'the intervention has no effect'
choices.feedback: Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence unless the CI excludes meaningful effects.

end1.text: Your paper is published as an honest, informative study. Other researchers can include it in meta-analyses without bias.

end2.text: This path undermines trust in your work. Review preregistration, deviations reporting and null-result interpretation.

quiz.q: HARKing means:
options: Presenting post-hoc hypotheses as if they were a priori
quiz.why: HARKing is Hypothesising After the Results are Known: presenting post-hoc hypotheses as if they were a priori (Kerr, 1998).

quiz.q: Registered Reports are peer-reviewed:
quiz.why: Registered Reports are peer-reviewed before data collection (Stage 1), so acceptance does not depend on the results.

quiz.q: Specification curve analysis shows:
options: Results across many reasonable analytic choices
quiz.why: Specification curve analysis shows results across many reasonable analytic choices, which tests robustness. It does not pick one best model or show only significant ones.

quiz.q: Which multiple-comparison approach controls the false discovery rate?
quiz.why: Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate. Bonferroni, Holm and Tukey control familywise error.

scenes.text: Aditya submits his thesis analysis. Six months later, an examiner asks him to rerun one model with an extra covariate.
He can't. The Excel file was edited by hand, the code is spread across 'final_v3_REAL.R' files, and a package update changed results.
His lab mate Mariam's project reruns from raw data to every figure with one command.
Reproducibility isn't extra work at the end; it's how you work from day one.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Computational reproducibility:** same data + same code → same results
- **Replicability:** new data, same methods → consistent results
- **Robustness:** same data, different reasonable analyses → consistent results
- **Generalisability:** different populations/settings

The first is fully within your control.

steps.title: Project structure and scripts
steps.body:
```
project/
  data/raw/        (read-only, never edited by hand)
  data/processed/  (created by scripts)
  code/            (01_clean.R, 02_models.R, 03_figures.R)
  outputs/         (tables, figures)
  docs/            (preregistration, codebook, README)
```
- Every transformation in **code**, not manual spreadsheet edits
- Literate programming (R Markdown/Quarto, Jupyter) to weave code and text
- Set random seeds; record software and package versions (renv, conda, requirements.txt; containers like Docker for long-term)
- A README that says how to run everything

steps.title: Version control and data management
steps.body:
- **Git** tracks every change; commit small, meaningful changes with clear messages; host on GitHub/GitLab (private until publication if needed)
- **Data management plan:** storage, backups (3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site), access control, retention
- **FAIR principles** (Wilkinson et al., 2016): Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — share data and code in repositories (OSF, Zenodo, Dataverse) with persistent identifiers (DOIs) and licences
- **Sensitive data:** de-identify, consider synthetic data or controlled access; follow consent terms and India's DPDP Act 2023 where applicable

steps.title: Worked minimal reproducible checklist
steps.body:
Before submitting a paper:
1. Fresh clone of the repository on another computer
2. Install dependencies from the lockfile
3. Run the master script
4. Confirm every number in the manuscript matches outputs (ideally numbers are inserted by code)
5. Archive the exact version (Zenodo DOI) and cite it in the paper

Many journals now ask for data and code availability statements; some run reproducibility checks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hand-editing raw data.
- Copying numbers manually into Word.
- Sharing code without the environment it needs.
- Putting identifiable participant data in a public repository.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create the folder structure above for your current project, initialise a Git repository, and write a 10-line README explaining how to reproduce one figure.

activity.prompt: Reproducibility checklist for your thesis project
items: Raw data stored read-only with a backup in a second location
All cleaning and analysis done in scripts
Project under Git version control with regular commits
Package versions recorded (lockfile or environment file)
Random seeds set for any simulation or resampling
README explains how to run everything from scratch
Data and code archived with a DOI at publication (respecting consent and privacy)

quiz.q: Computational reproducibility means:
options: New data give the same result
Same data and code give the same results
quiz.why: Computational reproducibility means the same data and code give the same results. New data giving the same result is replication.

quiz.q: FAIR stands for:
quiz.why: FAIR stands for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable, the data principles of Wilkinson et al.

quiz.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule means:
quiz.why: The 3-2-1 backup rule means 3 copies, on 2 media, with 1 off-site, to protect data.

quiz.q: Which practice most threatens reproducibility?
options: Hand-editing raw data in a spreadsheet
quiz.why: Hand-editing raw data in a spreadsheet most threatens reproducibility because changes are untraceable. Scripts, Git and recording package versions help.

questions.q: Cohen's d is:
questions.why: Cohen's d is a standardised mean difference, the difference between means divided by a standard deviation. It is not an odds ratio, correlation or p-value.

questions.q: Preregistration is a:
questions.why: Preregistration is a time-stamped research plan made before data are seen. It is not an ethics form, a publication or a repository.

questions.q: Power is the probability of:
questions.why: Power is the probability of detecting a true effect, 1 − β. It is not the Type I error rate.

questions.q: Counts with variance much larger than the mean suggest:
questions.why: Counts whose variance is much larger than the mean show overdispersion, so negative binomial regression fits better than a Poisson, t-test or linear regression.

questions.q: Optional stopping without correction is a form of:
questions.why: Optional stopping without correction, checking repeatedly and stopping when p < .05, is p-hacking because it inflates false positives.

questions.q: Approximate n per group for d = 0.4, 80% power, α = 0.05:
questions.why: n ≈ 15.7/d² = 15.7/0.16 ≈ 98, about 100 per group.

questions.q: In a cluster-randomised trial, the effective sample size is driven heavily by:
options: Number of clusters and the ICC
questions.why: In cluster-randomised trials, the effective sample size depends heavily on the number of clusters and the ICC, through the design effect. Number of individuals alone is not what matters.

questions.q: Scheel et al. (2021) compared positive-result rates in Registered Reports vs standard reports:
questions.why: Scheel et al. (2021) found about 44% positive results in Registered Reports versus about 96% in standard reports, evidence of publication bias.

questions.q: Type M error (Gelman & Carlin) refers to:
questions.why: A Type M (magnitude) error is an exaggerated magnitude of a significant estimate (Gelman and Carlin). It differs from a wrong-sign error.

questions.q: Median splits on a continuous predictor typically:
options: Reduce power and can create spurious effects
questions.why: Median splits throw away information, so they reduce power and can create spurious effects. Avoid dichotomising continuous predictors.

questions.q: Treating stimuli as a random factor (Judd, Westfall & Kenny) matters because:
options: Effects should generalise beyond the sampled stimuli
questions.why: Treating stimuli as a random factor matters because effects should generalise beyond the sampled stimuli (Judd, Westfall and Kenny). Ignoring this increases false positives.

questions.q: Two one-sided tests (TOST) are used to:
questions.why: Two one-sided tests (TOST) establish equivalence within bounds. They are not for detecting any effect or computing power.

questions.q: Under MNAR missingness, multiple imputation assuming MAR:
options: May be biased; sensitivity analyses are needed
questions.why: Under MNAR missingness, imputation assuming MAR may be biased, so sensitivity analyses are needed. It does not remove all bias.

courses.title: Research Ethics, Integrity, Thesis Writing and Publishing
courses.summary: Doing research rightly and getting it read: ethics review and informed consent, academic integrity and authorship, writing a thesis chapter by chapter, and navigating journals, peer review and open science.
outcomes: Learners can prepare an ethics application addressing consent, risk, confidentiality and vulnerable groups
Learners can recognise fabrication, falsification, plagiarism and authorship misconduct, and use AI tools transparently
Learners can structure a thesis and write clear chapters with a coherent argument
Learners can choose journals, avoid predatory publishers and write cover letters
Learners can respond constructively to peer review and understand preprints and open access

story.title: Consent in a language she couldn't read

scenes.text: Kavya plans a study on maternal health in tribal villages of Chhattisgarh. Her consent form is four pages of English legal text.
The Institutional Ethics Committee sends it back: 'Participants must understand what they agree to.'
She creates an audio consent in Gondi and Chhattisgarhi, a one-page picture sheet, and a process for community-level permission plus individual consent.
Ethics isn't a form to clear; it's respect built into the design.

steps.title: Where modern research ethics came from
steps.body:
- **Nuremberg Code (1947):** after Nazi medical experiments — voluntary consent is essential.
- **Declaration of Helsinki** (World Medical Association, 1964, revised several times).
- **Tuskegee syphilis study** (USA, 1932–1972): Black men were left untreated even after penicillin became standard — a defining scandal.
- **Belmont Report (1979):** three principles — **respect for persons** (autonomy, consent, protection of those with diminished autonomy), **beneficence** (maximise benefits, minimise harms), **justice** (fair distribution of burdens and benefits).
- **India:** ICMR's **National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (2017)**; the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, for drug trials; registration of trials in **CTRI**. Social science research is reviewed by institutional ethics committees following similar principles.

steps.title: Informed consent
steps.body:
Elements: purpose, procedures, duration, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, voluntariness, **right to withdraw without penalty**, contact details.
- **Comprehension** matters more than signatures: plain language, local language, verbal/audio consent where literacy is limited (with a witness where required)
- **Assent** from children plus parental/guardian consent
- **Community consent** may be culturally appropriate but never replaces individual consent
- Deception studies require justification, minimal risk and debriefing

steps.title: Risk, confidentiality and vulnerable groups
steps.body:
- Risks include psychological distress, social harm (stigma, being identified), legal risk and economic loss — not just physical harm.
- **Vulnerable groups:** children, prisoners, people with cognitive impairment, people in dependent relationships (your own students or employees), marginalised communities — need extra safeguards.
- **Confidentiality:** de-identification, secure storage, limits of confidentiality (e.g., mandatory reporting of child abuse under POCSO in India) explained up front.
- **Data protection:** India's DPDP Act 2023; GDPR if you handle EU residents' data.
- **Online and social media data:** public ≠ fair game; consider expectations of privacy and re-identification from quotes.

steps.title: Worked: ethics application essentials
steps.body:
1. Background and justification (why the knowledge is worth the burden)
2. Design, sample, recruitment (who approaches whom; avoid coercion)
3. Consent process and materials (with translations)
4. Risks and mitigation (distress protocol with referral, e.g., Tele-MANAS 14416)
5. Benefits (to participants, communities, knowledge) and compensation
6. Data management, confidentiality, retention and sharing plan
7. Conflicts of interest and funding
8. Plans for dissemination back to participants/communities

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting data collection before approval (including 'pilots').
- Recruiting your own students without safeguards against pressure.
- Promising 'complete anonymity' in a small community.
- Treating ethics approval as a one-time event; amendments are needed when protocols change.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rewrite the first paragraph of a consent form for your study at a Class 6 reading level. Read it aloud to someone outside academia and ask them to explain it back.

statements.s: The Belmont Report's three principles are respect for persons, beneficence and justice.
statements.why: 1979 report.

statements.s: Community leaders' permission can replace individual informed consent.
statements.why: It may complement, never replace, individual consent.

statements.s: Children's research typically needs parental consent and the child's assent.
statements.why: Both are expected.

statements.s: Publicly visible social media posts can always be quoted verbatim without ethical consideration.
statements.why: Re-identification and privacy expectations matter.

statements.s: A small pilot study can begin before ethics approval if it's informal.
statements.why: Research with human participants needs approval first.

quiz.q: The Tuskegee study is infamous because:
options: Participants were denied effective treatment and deceived
quiz.why: The Tuskegee study is infamous because participants were denied effective treatment and deceived, a major ethics violation. It was not a survey or preregistered.

quiz.q: ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for biomedical and health research were issued in:
quiz.why: ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for biomedical and health research were issued in 2017 (with an earlier 2006 version).

quiz.q: Recruiting your own students raises concerns about:
quiz.why: Recruiting your own students raises concerns about coercion or undue influence because of the dependent relationship. It is not mainly a power or measurement issue.

quiz.q: 'Beneficence' requires researchers to:
quiz.why: Beneficence requires researchers to maximise benefits and minimise harms (Belmont). It does not require RCTs or payment.

scenes.text: Arnav runs his thesis chapter through the university's similarity checker: 38% match.
He panics. Most of it is his own published paper, a standard methods description and properly quoted definitions — but two paragraphs were paraphrased too closely from a review.
His supervisor explains how to read the report, cite his own prior work, and rewrite in his own synthesis.
Integrity is about honesty and attribution, not gaming a percentage.

steps.title: Research misconduct: FFP
steps.body:
- **Fabrication:** making up data or results
- **Falsification:** manipulating materials, equipment, processes, or changing/omitting data so the record misrepresents the research (including image manipulation)
- **Plagiarism:** using others' ideas, words, data or images without appropriate credit — including **self-plagiarism** (reusing your published text without citation) and translated plagiarism

Diederik Stapel, a prominent social psychologist, was found in 2011 to have fabricated data across many studies, leading to dozens of retractions. Retraction Watch tracks retractions worldwide.

steps.title: Indian regulations
steps.body:
The **UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018** define similarity levels for theses and papers, excluding quoted, referenced and common-knowledge material:
- Level 0: up to 10% — minor
- Level 1: above 10% to 40%
- Level 2: above 40% to 60%
- Level 3: above 60%
with escalating consequences for higher levels. Universities must use plagiarism-detection software and set up academic integrity panels. Similarity software flags overlap; humans judge whether it is plagiarism.

steps.title: Authorship
steps.body:
**ICMJE criteria** (widely used in biomedicine and beyond): authors should meet all four:
1. Substantial contributions to conception/design, or data acquisition, analysis or interpretation
2. Drafting or critically revising for important intellectual content
3. Final approval of the version to be published
4. Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work

Problems: **gift/honorary** authorship (head of department added without contribution), **ghost** authorship (writers omitted), coercive authorship. The **CRediT** taxonomy lists 14 contributor roles (e.g., conceptualisation, formal analysis, writing – original draft) to make contributions transparent. Discuss authorship order early and revisit it.

steps.title: Using generative AI tools
steps.body:
Common positions of publishers and bodies such as COPE (as of recent guidance; check your target journal's current policy):
- AI tools **cannot be authors** — they can't take responsibility
- **Disclose** substantive use (e.g., in methods or acknowledgements)
- You remain responsible for accuracy: AI can fabricate references and facts
- Don't upload confidential data or manuscripts under review into public tools
- Many universities have their own rules for theses — read them

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Patchwriting': swapping synonyms in someone else's sentences.
- Citing a source you haven't read, copied from another paper's reference list.
- Trimming 'outliers' without a pre-specified rule and without reporting it.
- Adding a senior colleague as author 'out of respect'.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take one paragraph from a key paper. Close it. Write what *you* understand and how it relates to other work, then cite it. Compare: is your text a synthesis or a paraphrase?

activity.prompt: Classify each action.

items.text: Quoting a definition in quotation marks with a citation
Reusing your published methods paragraph without citing your earlier paper
Inventing survey responses to reach the target sample
Using an AI tool to polish grammar and disclosing it per journal policy
Removing data points that contradict your hypothesis without reporting it
Adding the department head as co-author though they did not contribute
Copying a figure from another paper without permission or credit

quiz.q: FFP stands for:
quiz.why: FFP stands for Fabrication, Falsification and Plagiarism, the core forms of research misconduct.

quiz.q: Under UGC 2018 regulations, Level 0 similarity is:
quiz.why: Under the UGC 2018 regulations, Level 0 similarity is up to 10%. It is treated as minor similarity.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an ICMJE authorship criterion?
quiz.why: Being head of department is not an ICMJE authorship criterion, because position alone does not qualify. Substantial contribution, drafting or revising, final approval and accountability do.

quiz.q: Generative AI tools listed as co-authors are:
options: Generally not accepted because they can't take responsibility
quiz.why: Generative AI tools listed as co-authors are generally not accepted because they cannot take responsibility for the work (publisher and COPE positions).

story.title: The blank page in year three

scenes.text: In her third year, Dr.-to-be Anjali in Pune has data, results and 40 pages of notes — but no chapter.
Her supervisor asks her to write a one-page 'argument map': the question, the answer, and how each chapter gets there.
She writes 500 words a day, shares rough drafts every two weeks, and revises structure before polishing sentences.
Eighteen months later she submits — and her examiners praise the thesis's clear through-line.

steps.title: Thesis structures
steps.body:
- **Monograph (traditional):** Introduction → Literature review → Methodology → Results/Findings chapters → Discussion → Conclusion
- **Thesis by publication / papers-based:** introduction and integrative chapters around published or submitted papers — check your university's rules on co-authored papers and declarations

Either way, the thesis must make an **original contribution** and present a coherent **argument**, not a diary of everything you did.

steps.title: Chapter by chapter
steps.body:
- **Introduction:** problem, gap, aims/questions, contribution, roadmap
