- **Literature review:** an argument that leads to your questions (synthesis by theme; end each section with the gap)
- **Methodology:** design, sample, measures/data sources, procedures, analysis, ethics, limitations, positionality where relevant — enough detail for replication
- **Results/Findings:** report, don't interpret excessively; tables and figures with clear captions
- **Discussion:** answer the questions; compare with literature; explain unexpected findings; limitations; implications for theory, practice, policy
- **Conclusion:** contribution in plain terms; future research

Write the **abstract** last: problem, method, key findings, contribution.

steps.title: Writing well
steps.body:
- One idea per paragraph; topic sentence first ('signposting')
- Prefer clear, active sentences; define terms once and use them consistently
- **Hedge appropriately:** 'suggests', 'is consistent with' for correlational evidence
- Figures: one message each; label axes with units; colour-blind-friendly palettes
- Use a reference manager and one citation style consistently
- Reverse outline after drafting: list each paragraph's point to check flow

steps.title: Process and working with supervisors
steps.body:
- **Write early:** methods and literature drafts in year 1–2
- Daily or weekly writing targets (time or words); protect writing hours
- Share drafts with specific questions ('Is the argument in section 2 convincing?')
- Keep a meeting log with agreed actions and deadlines
- Build a timeline backwards from submission, including time for supervisor feedback, formatting, similarity checking and binding
- For the **viva/defence**: know your contribution, limitations and why you made each methodological choice; practise with mock vivas

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Literature review as an annotated bibliography.
- Discussion that merely repeats results.
- Over-claiming causality or generalisability.
- Leaving formatting and references until the last week.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your thesis argument in five sentences: (1) the problem, (2) the gap, (3) what you did, (4) what you found, (5) why it matters. Pin it above your desk.

activity.prompt: Order the chapters of a traditional monograph thesis.

quiz.q: The abstract is usually best written:
quiz.why: The abstract is usually best written last, after the argument and findings are settled. Writing it first risks it not matching the final work.

quiz.q: A literature review chapter should mainly:
options: Build an argument leading to your questions
quiz.why: A literature review chapter should build an argument leading to your research questions, not catalogue every paper or report results.

quiz.q: The discussion chapter should:
options: Interpret findings, relate to literature, address limitations and implications
quiz.why: The discussion should interpret findings, relate them to the literature and address limitations and implications. It should not merely repeat results or add new data.

quiz.q: A 'reverse outline' helps you:
options: Check the logical flow by listing each paragraph's main point
quiz.why: A reverse outline lists each paragraph's main point afterwards, to check logical flow. It is not for references, word counts or avoiding plagiarism software.

story.title: The email promising publication in 7 days

scenes.text: Rakesh receives an email: 'Dear Esteemed Researcher, publish in our International Journal of Advanced Everything within 7 days. Fee: $99.'
His paper has just been rejected elsewhere. It's tempting.
His supervisor checks: no real editorial board, fake impact metrics, not indexed in the databases it claims.
Instead, they revise using the reviewers' comments and submit to a reputable journal. It's accepted after one round of major revisions.

steps.title: Choosing a journal
steps.body:
- Scope fit: read recent issues; are papers like yours published there?
- Audience: disciplinary vs interdisciplinary; Indian vs international
- Indexing (Scopus, Web of Science), editorial board credibility, review times, open-access options and fees (APCs)
- Use journal-finder tools from publishers cautiously; ask senior colleagues

**Predatory journals** feature aggressive spam, promises of very fast acceptance, fake metrics, little or sham peer review and hidden fees. Tools: **Think. Check. Submit.**; verify indexing claims directly on the database. UGC's approach to approved-journal lists has changed over the years, so check UGC's and your institution's current guidance.

steps.title: Submitting
steps.body:
- Follow author guidelines exactly (word limits, structure, reference style, data availability statements, reporting checklists: CONSORT for trials, STROBE for observational studies, PRISMA for reviews, COREQ/SRQR for qualitative research)
- **Cover letter:** what the paper shows, why it fits this journal, confirmation it's not under review elsewhere, any conflicts of interest
- Suggest reviewers if invited (no conflicts)
- **Preprints** (arXiv, PsyArXiv, SSRN, medRxiv, OSF Preprints) share findings early; most journals accept preprinted submissions — check policy

steps.title: Peer review
steps.body:
Models: single-blind, double-blind, open review (names and/or reports published), post-publication review.
Outcomes: desk reject, reject, major revision, minor revision, accept. Desk rejection is common and often about fit, not quality.

Peer review improves papers but misses errors and has biases; it doesn't certify truth. Reviewing for others is part of scholarly citizenship — follow COPE's ethical guidelines for peer reviewers (confidentiality, declare conflicts, constructive tone).

steps.title: Worked response to reviewers
steps.body:
Format: a point-by-point table.
- **Reviewer 1, Comment 3:** 'The sample is not representative.'
- **Response:** 'Thank you. We agree this limits generalisation. We have (a) added a comparison of our sample with census data (new Table S2), (b) reweighted estimates as a robustness check (Section 4.3), and (c) expanded the limitations (p. 18, lines 402–415).'

Rules: thank, respond to every point, show exactly what changed and where, disagree politely with evidence when needed, and keep tone professional even with harsh reviews.

steps.title: Open science and after publication
steps.body:
- **Open access:** gold (published OA, often with APC), green (self-archived accepted manuscript), diamond (no fees for authors or readers)
- Licences such as CC BY
- Share data/code (FAIR) and materials
- **Corrections and retractions:** if you find an error, contact the journal promptly — correcting the record is a mark of integrity
- Communicate findings to the public and to participants in accessible language

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Simultaneous submission to multiple journals (not allowed).
- Salami slicing: splitting one study into many thin papers.
- Ignoring reviewer comments in resubmission elsewhere — the same reviewers may see it again.
- Paying for 'guaranteed publication' services.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick three candidate journals for your next paper. For each, note scope fit, indexing (verified on the database), typical review time and OA options. Run each through the Think. Check. Submit. checklist.

a.text: You receive 'major revisions'. Reviewer 2 is blunt and asks for an extra analysis you think is unnecessary. What do you do first?

choices.label: Write an angry reply and withdraw
choices.feedback: Emotional responses rarely help; sleep on it.

choices.label: Wait a day, then list every comment and plan a response for each

b.text: For the requested extra analysis, you run it. Results are consistent with your main findings. How do you report it?

choices.label: Add it as a robustness check in the supplement and reference it in the response
choices.feedback: Shows responsiveness and strengthens the paper.

choices.label: Say you ran it but not include it anywhere

c.text: Another comment is factually mistaken about your method. How do you respond?

choices.label: Politely clarify with evidence, and revise the text so future readers don't make the same mistake
Tell the reviewer they clearly didn't read the paper

end1.text: The editor accepts your revision with minor changes. Your paper is clearer and more robust.

end2.text: The process stalls. Review how to write a point-by-point response with a professional tone.

quiz.q: A hallmark of a predatory journal is:
options: Promises of acceptance within days and spam invitations
quiz.why: Promises of acceptance within days and spam invitations are red flags of a predatory journal. A known editorial board, verified indexing and rigorous peer review are good signs.

quiz.q: STROBE is a reporting guideline for:
quiz.why: STROBE is the reporting guideline for observational studies in epidemiology. RCTs use CONSORT and systematic reviews use PRISMA.

quiz.q: Green open access means:
options: Self-archiving an accepted manuscript in a repository
quiz.why: Green open access means self-archiving an accepted manuscript in a repository. Paying an article processing charge is gold OA, and diamond OA has no fees.

quiz.q: Submitting the same manuscript to two journals at once is:
quiz.why: Submitting the same manuscript to two journals at once is not permitted because it is duplicate submission.

questions.q: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice come from:
questions.why: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice are the principles of the Belmont Report (1979). CONSORT is a trial-reporting guideline.

questions.q: Plagiarism includes:
options: Using others' words or ideas without credit
questions.why: Plagiarism is using others' words or ideas without credit. Quoting or paraphrasing with citation and citing your own work are acceptable.

questions.q: Which chapter describes design, sampling and analysis?
questions.why: The methodology chapter describes the design, sampling and analysis. Introduction, discussion and conclusion do other work.

questions.q: CONSORT is the reporting guideline for:
questions.why: CONSORT is the reporting guideline for randomised controlled trials, not for case reports, surveys or qualitative research.

questions.q: A distress protocol in a sensitive interview study should include:
options: Pausing, offering support and referral options
questions.why: A distress protocol should include pausing, offering support and referral options, to protect participant welfare. Continuing regardless or just deleting data is not adequate.

questions.q: Gift authorship is:
options: Listing someone who didn't meet authorship criteria
questions.why: Gift authorship is listing someone who did not meet authorship criteria, also called honorary authorship. Sharing first authorship or acknowledging funders is different.

questions.q: Similarity of 25% under UGC 2018 falls in:
questions.why: Under UGC 2018, similarity of 10–40% is Level 1, so 25% falls in Level 1. Level 0 is up to 10%.

questions.q: The CRediT taxonomy is used to:
questions.why: The CRediT taxonomy describes each contributor's role in a paper. It does not measure citations, rank journals or check plagiarism.

questions.q: Falsification includes:
options: Selectively omitting data or manipulating images so the record is misrepresented
questions.why: Falsification includes selectively omitting data or manipulating images so the record is misrepresented. Making up data is fabrication, a distinct form.

questions.q: When a reviewer is factually wrong, the best response is to:
options: Clarify politely with evidence and improve the text
Complain to the editor about the reviewer
questions.why: When a reviewer is factually wrong, clarify politely with evidence and improve the text so it is not misread. Ignoring, withdrawing or complaining about the reviewer is less professional.

questions.q: Diamond open access means:
options: No fees for authors or readers
questions.why: Diamond open access means no fees for authors or readers, often funded by societies or institutions. It is not embargoed or fee-heavy.

questions.q: Why should confidential manuscripts under review not be pasted into public AI tools?
options: It breaches confidentiality of peer review
questions.why: Confidential manuscripts under review should not be pasted into public AI tools because that breaches the confidentiality of peer review (COPE and publisher guidance). It is not about length or speed.

questions.q: Salami slicing refers to:
options: Splitting one study into multiple minimal publications
questions.why: Salami slicing is splitting one study into multiple minimal publications, which is redundant publication. It is not preprinting, meta-analysis or data sharing.

research-psychology-advanced.title: Advanced Psychology for Experts (Shodh)
research-psychology-advanced.description: A research-level refresher for professors, clinicians and doctoral scholars: attachment and lifespan development, cognition, emotion and decision science, social influence and personality science, and the replication crisis — with classic researchers cited and contested findings clearly marked.

courses.title: Attachment and Lifespan Development: An Expert Refresher
courses.summary: A precise, research-level review of attachment theory from Bowlby to adult attachment dimensions, early adversity and plasticity, adolescence and emerging adulthood, and ageing — with effect sizes and contested points flagged.
outcomes: Learners can state the core propositions of attachment theory and the evidence for and against intergenerational transmission
Learners can compare categorical and dimensional models of adult attachment and their measurement (AAI vs self-report)
Learners can evaluate evidence on early adversity, sensitive periods and differential susceptibility
Learners can critique dual-systems models of adolescence and the social-media debate
Learners can explain lifespan theories of ageing: SOC, socioemotional selectivity and cognitive change

lessons.title: Attachment theory: propositions, measurement and transmission

story.title: A professor's refresher before a seminar

scenes.text: Prof. Rukmini Iyer, who has taught developmental psychology for 25 years in Chennai, prepares a doctoral seminar on attachment.
Her lecture notes still say 'attachment style is fixed by age two'. A student has emailed a meta-analysis showing only moderate stability.
She revisits the evidence: what Bowlby actually claimed, what Ainsworth measured, what the AAI and later meta-analyses found.
Her updated seminar is more nuanced — and more interesting.

steps.title: Core propositions (Bowlby, 1969/1973/1980)
steps.body:
- Infants possess an evolved **attachment behavioural system** that promotes proximity to caregivers under threat; caregivers serve as a **safe haven** and **secure base**.
- Repeated interactions are represented as **internal working models (IWMs)** of self and others, guiding expectations and behaviour.
- Separation responses follow protest → despair → detachment (Robertson & Bowlby's observations of hospitalised children).
- Attachment is distinct from feeding (Harlow's rhesus monkey work) and from temperament, though they interact.

steps.title: Measurement across the lifespan
steps.body:
- **Strange Situation Procedure** (Ainsworth et al., 1978; 12–20 months): secure (B), avoidant (A), resistant/ambivalent (C); **disorganised (D)** added by Main & Solomon (1986, 1990). In low-risk samples, roughly 60–65% are classified secure.
- **Attachment Q-Sort** (Waters & Deane): observational, continuous security score.
- **Adult Attachment Interview** (George, Kaplan & Main, 1985): semi-structured; coded for **coherence of discourse** about childhood, not content — secure/autonomous, dismissing, preoccupied, unresolved.
- **Self-report** romantic attachment (Hazan & Shaver, 1987; Bartholomew & Horowitz's four categories, 1991; **ECR** by Brennan, Clark & Shaver, 1998, with two dimensions: **anxiety** and **avoidance**).

**AAI and self-report measures correlate only weakly** — they tap different constructs (state of mind about early attachment vs conscious feelings in close relationships). Don't use them interchangeably.

steps.title: Key quantitative findings
steps.body:
- **Sensitivity → security:** De Wolff & van IJzendoorn (1997) meta-analysis: r ≈ 0.24 — significant but modest.
- **Intergenerational transmission:** van IJzendoorn (1995): parental AAI predicts infant SSP classification (concordance around 75% for secure/insecure), but sensitivity explains only part of it — the **'transmission gap'**. Later IPD meta-analysis (Verhage et al., 2016) found a smaller pooled association than early studies and evidence that effects have declined over time.
- **Stability:** Fraley (2002) estimated moderate stability from infancy to later ages (around r ≈ 0.39), consistent with a 'prototype' plus change; Pinquart, Feußner & Ahnert (2013) also found moderate stability, lower over longer intervals and in high-risk samples.
- **Outcomes:** insecurity (especially disorganisation) predicts externalising problems (Fearon et al., 2010, d ≈ 0.31); associations with internalising are smaller (Groh et al., 2012, d ≈ 0.15).

steps.title: Contested and nuanced points
steps.body:
- **Determinism:** early attachment is a probabilistic risk/protective factor, not destiny; later relationships and contexts matter.
- **Cross-cultural validity:** van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg (1988) found secure was modal across countries, with more avoidance in some Western European samples and more resistance in Israeli kibbutz and Japanese samples. Critics (e.g., Heidi Keller; Rothbaum et al., 2000) argue the 'sensitivity' construct and SSP norms reflect Western middle-class caregiving, and multiple-caregiver systems (common in India) need different models.
- **Disorganisation misuse:** disorganised classification is *not* a diagnostic marker of maltreatment for individual children; a 2017 consensus statement (Granqvist et al.) warned against using it in child-protection decisions.
- **Attachment therapy:** coercive 'holding therapies' are harmful and not supported by evidence.

steps.title: Applying the IWM idea carefully
steps.body: A dismissing AAI state of mind (idealising parents without supporting memories; 'I don't remember much') predicts, probabilistically, a more avoidant infant SSP pattern. The theorised mechanism is parental sensitivity — but given the transmission gap, consider other routes: mentalisation/reflective functioning (Fonagy, Slade), mind-mindedness (Meins), shared genes and context. Twin studies of infant attachment suggest modest heritability compared with shared environment, though findings vary by measure and age (e.g., later childhood and adolescence show larger genetic influence).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draft one seminar slide titled 'What attachment research does NOT show', listing three common overclaims with the study that corrects each.

activity.prompt: Match each finding to its source.

quiz.q: The AAI is coded mainly for:
options: Coherence of discourse about attachment experiences
quiz.why: The Adult Attachment Interview is coded mainly for coherence of discourse about attachment experiences (Main's system), not for the content of memories.

quiz.q: The correlation between AAI and self-report romantic attachment measures is:
quiz.why: Correlations between the AAI and self-report romantic attachment measures are weak, because they tap different constructs.

quiz.q: The 'transmission gap' refers to:
options: Parents' AAI not predicting infant attachment
Sensitivity explaining only part of AAI–infant concordance
quiz.why: The 'transmission gap' is that parental sensitivity explains only part of the AAI–infant attachment concordance (van IJzendoorn, 1995). It does not mean no prediction at all.

quiz.q: A 2017 consensus statement warned against using disorganised attachment to:
quiz.why: A 2017 consensus statement (Granqvist et al.) warned against using disorganised attachment to make individual child-protection decisions, because it is not diagnostic of maltreatment for individuals.

lessons.title: Early adversity, sensitive periods and plasticity

story.title: Two children from the same orphanage

scenes.text: In the 1990s and 2000s, researchers studied children raised in Romanian state institutions with severe psychosocial deprivation.
In the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, children were randomly assigned to high-quality foster care or continued institutional care.
Children placed earlier showed better outcomes on several measures than those placed later.
Dr. Arvind Menon, a child psychiatrist in Kochi, rereads the findings before testifying on adoption policy.

steps.title: Natural and randomised experiments
steps.body:
- **English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) study** (Rutter, Sonuga-Barke and colleagues): children adopted into UK families after institutional deprivation. Deprivation lasting beyond about 6 months was associated with persistent problems in a subset (a 'deprivation-specific' pattern: quasi-autism, disinhibited social engagement, cognitive impairment, inattention/overactivity), followed into adulthood. Many children nevertheless showed remarkable recovery.
- **Bucharest Early Intervention Project (BEIP)** (Nelson, Fox & Zeanah; started 2000): the first RCT of foster care vs institutional care. Foster care improved IQ, language, attachment security, and some EEG measures; benefits were generally larger with earlier placement (often before roughly 24 months for some outcomes).

steps.title: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs)
steps.body:
Felitti et al. (1998), Kaiser–CDC study: a dose–response association between the number of ACE categories (abuse, neglect, household dysfunction) and adult health risks.

**Cautions:** ACE scores are retrospective, give equal weight to very different events, and are good for population-level risk but **poor for individual prediction** (Baldwin et al., 2021, *JAMA Psychiatry*). Screening individuals with ACE scores is contested. Prospective and retrospective reports of maltreatment show limited agreement (Baldwin et al., 2019).

steps.title: Differential susceptibility
steps.body:
**Diathesis–stress** says some individuals are more vulnerable to adversity. **Differential susceptibility** (Belsky; Belsky & Pluess, 2009) and **biological sensitivity to context** (Boyce & Ellis, 2005) propose that the same traits (e.g., negative emotionality, certain genotypes) make individuals more sensitive to *both* bad and good environments — 'orchids' vs 'dandelions'.

**Contested:** many early gene × environment findings (e.g., candidate-gene studies such as 5-HTTLPR × stress → depression, Caspi et al., 2003) did not hold up in large-scale analyses (Border et al., 2019). Phenotypic susceptibility and polygenic approaches are more promising but effects are small.

steps.title: Longitudinal cohorts to know
steps.body:
- **Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study** (New Zealand, born 1972–73): childhood self-control predicted adult health, wealth and crime (Moffitt et al., 2011)
- **NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development** (USA): child-care quality and quantity effects were mostly small; family factors predicted more
- **Young Lives** (including Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in India): poverty, nutrition and schooling across childhood
- **ALSPAC** (UK, 'Children of the 90s')

steps.title: Contested points
steps.body:
- Sensitive periods vary by domain; 'the first 1,000 days' is a useful policy frame but plasticity continues across life.
- Brain-imaging differences in deprived groups are associational and often small at the individual level.
- The marshmallow-test narrative of early self-control was weakened when Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018) found associations with later achievement were about half the original and largely attenuated after controlling for family background and early cognitive ability.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: You're asked whether a district should screen every child for ACEs and refer high scorers. Write a 100-word evidence-based answer covering population vs individual prediction and service availability.

statements.s: BEIP randomly assigned institutionalised children to foster care or continued institutional care.
statements.why: It is the key RCT in this area.

statements.s: ACE scores predict individual adult outcomes with high accuracy.
statements.why: They are population-level risk indicators with poor individual prediction.

statements.s: Large-scale genetic analyses supported the 5-HTTLPR × stress → depression hypothesis.
statements.why: Border et al. (2019) found no support for candidate-gene hypotheses including this one.

statements.s: Differential susceptibility predicts sensitive individuals benefit more from supportive environments.
statements.why: For better and for worse.

statements.s: Watts et al. (2018) found the marshmallow-test association with later achievement grew stronger with controls.
statements.why: It shrank substantially.

quiz.q: The ERA study found persistent problems were more common when deprivation lasted beyond about:
quiz.why: The ERA study found persistent problems more common when deprivation lasted beyond about 6 months, with deprivation-specific patterns. The other durations are not the threshold.

quiz.q: Felitti et al. (1998) reported:
options: A dose–response association between ACE count and adult health risks
quiz.why: Felitti et al. (1998), the ACE study, reported a dose–response association between the number of adverse childhood experiences and adult health risks.

quiz.q: Boyce & Ellis's 'biological sensitivity to context' is closest to:
quiz.why: Boyce and Ellis's biological sensitivity to context is closest to differential susceptibility, the idea that some children are more affected by both bad and good environments (orchid/dandelion).

quiz.q: Which cohort includes children from Andhra Pradesh and Telangana?
quiz.why: Young Lives follows children in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, along with other countries. Dunedin, NICHD SECCYD and ALSPAC are in other places.

scenes.text: Dr. Fiona Mathew, a counselling psychologist in Bengaluru, is asked at a school talk: 'Is social media causing the teen mental-health crisis?'
One bestselling book says yes, emphatically. Several large data analyses say the average association is small.
She answers carefully: what's known, what's contested, and what parents can sensibly do now.
Adolescence research is full of strong claims; experts are those who know the evidence's limits.

steps.title: Dual-systems and imbalance models
steps.body:
**Steinberg's dual-systems model** and **Casey's imbalance model**: an earlier-maturing socioemotional/reward system (ventral striatum) and a later-maturing cognitive-control system (prefrontal cortex) create heightened sensation seeking in mid-adolescence, especially in emotionally 'hot' and peer contexts (Gardner & Steinberg, 2005, driving-game study: peers increased risk-taking in adolescents more than adults).

Cross-national evidence (Steinberg et al., 2018, 11 countries including India): sensation seeking peaked in late adolescence; self-regulation rose into the mid-20s.

**Critiques:** brain maturation is more continuous and network-based; much adolescent risk-taking is exploratory and adaptive; real-world risk depends heavily on opportunity and context (Romer et al.).

steps.title: Emerging adulthood
steps.body:
Jeffrey **Arnett (2000)** proposed 'emerging adulthood' (≈18–25/29) as a distinct period in industrialised societies: identity exploration, instability, self-focus, feeling in-between, possibilities.

Critics argue it describes mainly educated, middle-class youth and may be a cultural/economic period rather than a universal developmental stage. In India, extended education, delayed marriage in cities and family interdependence create varied patterns.

steps.title: The social media and mental-health debate (contested)
steps.body:
- **Concern side:** Twenge, Haidt and colleagues point to rising adolescent depression, anxiety and self-harm indicators in several countries from around 2012, coinciding with smartphone adoption, and to experimental and quasi-experimental studies (e.g., Facebook rollout across US colleges, Braghieri, Levy & Makarin, 2022).
- **Sceptical side:** Orben & Przybylski (2019) — specification curve analysis of large datasets found the average association between digital technology use and adolescent wellbeing was negative but very small (explaining at most about 0.4% of variance). Odgers and others note that correlational data cannot establish causation, effects may be heterogeneous, and other causes may contribute.
- **Where there's more agreement:** effects likely vary by person, platform, content and displacement of sleep; problematic use matters more than total time; cyberbullying and sleep loss are plausible mechanisms.

steps.title: How to communicate contested evidence
steps.body:
- Separate **what is known** (rising distress indicators in several countries; small average associations; heterogeneity) from **what is debated** (causal share of social media).
- Avoid moral panic and dismissal alike; recommend reasonable steps with low downside (protect sleep, phone-free meals, monitoring for cyberbullying, discussing content) while research continues.
- Note measurement problems: self-reported screen time is imprecise.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a 120-word answer to the parent's question that a peer reviewer from either 'side' would accept as fair.

a.text: At a school talk, a parent asks: 'Is social media definitely causing teen depression?' You are the expert. What do you say?

choices.label: 'Yes, the evidence is clear — ban phones until 18.'
'Researchers disagree on how much it causes; average links are small but some teens are harmed. Here's what's sensible now.'

b.text: A teacher who reads the research asks about the small average effect sizes. How do you correct yourself?

choices.label: Acknowledge the debate and distinguish average effects from harms to vulnerable subgroups
Dismiss the studies as industry-funded

c.text: What practical advice do you give?

choices.label: Protect sleep, keep phones out of bedrooms at night, talk about content and cyberbullying, and seek help if distress persists
Tell parents not to worry at all
choices.feedback: That ignores real harms some teens face.

end1.text: Parents leave with clear, balanced guidance. You modelled how experts communicate uncertainty.

end2.text: This answer misrepresents the evidence. Review both sides of the debate and try again.

quiz.q: Gardner & Steinberg (2005) found peer presence increased risk-taking most in:
quiz.why: In Gardner and Steinberg (2005), peer presence increased risk-taking most in adolescents, as seen in the driving-game study. Adults and older adults were less affected.

quiz.q: Orben & Przybylski (2019) used which method to examine many analytic choices?
quiz.why: Orben and Przybylski (2019) used specification curve analysis to examine the many analytic choices across large datasets, not an RCT or meta-analysis.

quiz.q: A key critique of 'emerging adulthood' is that it:
options: May describe mainly privileged, industrialised populations
quiz.why: A key critique of 'emerging adulthood' is that it may describe mainly privileged, industrialised populations, given its cultural and economic specificity. It is not about ageing.

quiz.q: Steinberg et al. (2018), across 11 countries, found self-regulation:
options: Continued to rise into the mid-20s
quiz.why: Steinberg et al. (2018), across 11 countries, found self-regulation kept rising into the mid-20s, showing later maturation of control.

scenes.text: Retired engineer Mr. Kulkarni, 70, in Pune starts violin lessons. He's slower to learn than his granddaughter but practises smarter.
He no longer remembers names as fast, yet his vocabulary and judgement are sharper than ever.
His wife notices he's happier than at 50, spending time with fewer, closer friends.
Lifespan psychology explains all three observations — and challenges stereotypes of decline.

steps.title: Cognitive change
steps.body:
- **Fluid vs crystallised intelligence** (Cattell; Horn & Cattell): fluid (novel reasoning, processing speed) declines gradually from early adulthood; crystallised (knowledge, vocabulary) is maintained or grows into later life.
- Salthouse's work: **processing speed** declines account for much age-related variance in cognition.
- **Seattle Longitudinal Study** (Schaie): longitudinal declines are later and smaller than cross-sectional comparisons suggest (cohort effects).
- Hartshorne & Germine (2015): different abilities peak at very different ages, from the late teens to the 60s/70s.
- **Cognitive reserve** (Stern): education and engagement may help people tolerate brain pathology; mechanisms are debated.

steps.title: Selection, Optimisation, Compensation (Baltes)
steps.body:
Paul and Margret Baltes's **SOC** model: successful ageing involves **selecting** priorities, **optimising** resources for them, and **compensating** for losses. Example: pianist Arthur Rubinstein reportedly played fewer pieces, practised them more, and slowed down before fast passages to create contrast.

Baltes's lifespan principles: development is lifelong, multidimensional, multidirectional (gains and losses), plastic, and embedded in history and culture.

steps.title: Socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen)
steps.body:
When time horizons feel limited, people prioritise emotionally meaningful goals and close relationships over exploration. Predicts smaller but closer social networks with age.

**Positivity effect** (Mather & Carstensen, 2005): older adults attend to and remember positive relative to negative information more than younger adults do. Effect sizes vary across paradigms; a meta-analysis (Reed, Chan & Mikels, 2014) found a reliable but moderate effect, stronger when processing is unconstrained.

Emotional wellbeing often remains stable or improves into older age until very late life — the 'paradox of ageing'. Whether life satisfaction follows a U-shape across adulthood is **contested** and depends on controls and datasets.

steps.title: Contested and practical points
steps.body:
- **Brain-training games:** a 2014 consensus statement signed by many cognitive scientists and organised by two longevity/human-development research centres warned against claims that commercial games prevent decline; the large ACTIVE trial found trained abilities improved, with limited transfer to everyday function (some long-term findings, e.g., speed training and dementia risk, remain debated).
- **Physical activity, hearing correction, managing vascular risk and social engagement** have stronger evidence for supporting cognitive health; the *Lancet Commission* (2020, updated 2024) identifies modifiable risk factors for dementia.
- Ageism itself predicts worse outcomes (Levy's work on age stereotypes).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Apply SOC to your own career: which goals will you select, how will you optimise for them, and what will you compensate for as demands change?

cards.back: Fluid (novel reasoning, speed) declines gradually; crystallised (knowledge) is maintained or grows.
Limited time horizons shift goals towards emotional meaning and close ties (Carstensen).
Older adults' relative preference for positive over negative information (Mather & Carstensen, 2005).
Cross-sectional designs exaggerate decline because of cohort differences.
Education and engagement may buffer the clinical effects of brain pathology (Stern).

quiz.q: Which ability typically holds up best into older age?
quiz.why: Vocabulary (crystallised knowledge) typically holds up best into older age, while reaction time, processing speed and working memory span decline.

quiz.q: Cross-sectional studies of ageing tend to:
options: Overestimate decline due to cohort effects
quiz.why: Cross-sectional ageing studies tend to overestimate decline because of cohort effects (Schaie), as older cohorts differ in education and experience. Longitudinal data give a different picture.

quiz.q: Socioemotional selectivity theory predicts older adults' networks are:
quiz.why: Socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen) predicts older adults' networks are smaller and emotionally closer, because they prioritise meaningful relationships.

quiz.q: The 2014 scientists' consensus on brain-training games stated:
options: Claims of preventing decline were not supported
quiz.why: The 2014 consensus stated that claims brain-training games prevent cognitive decline were not supported, an overclaiming warning.

questions.q: An internal working model is:
options: A mental representation of self and others derived from attachment experiences
questions.why: An internal working model is a mental representation of self and others derived from attachment experiences (Bowlby). It is not a computer or statistical model.

questions.q: The ECR measures adult attachment on:
questions.why: The ECR measures adult attachment on two dimensions, anxiety and avoidance (Brennan et al., 1998), rather than categories.

questions.q: BEIP is notable as:
options: An RCT of foster vs institutional care
questions.why: The Bucharest Early Intervention Project (BEIP) is notable as an RCT of foster care versus continued institutional care. It was not an fMRI, survey or twin study.

questions.q: Arnett's emerging adulthood spans roughly:
questions.why: Arnett's emerging adulthood spans roughly ages 18 to 25/29 (Arnett, 2000).

questions.q: The SOC model was proposed by:
questions.why: The selection, optimisation and compensation (SOC) model was proposed by Baltes and Baltes. Carstensen is linked to socioemotional selectivity.

questions.q: De Wolff & van IJzendoorn's sensitivity–security association was about:
questions.why: De Wolff and van IJzendoorn found a modest sensitivity–security association of about r = 0.24, not a large one.

questions.q: Self-report romantic attachment and the AAI:
options: Correlate weakly and tap different constructs
questions.why: Self-report romantic attachment and the AAI correlate weakly because they tap different constructs. They are not interchangeable and do not measure infants.

questions.q: Large-scale genetic data (Border et al., 2019) found candidate-gene depression hypotheses:
questions.why: Large-scale genetic data (Border et al., 2019) did not support candidate-gene depression hypotheses, including 5-HTTLPR.

questions.q: Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018) found that marshmallow-test associations with later achievement:
options: Were about half the original and largely attenuated with controls
questions.why: Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018) found marshmallow-test associations with later achievement were about half the original and largely attenuated after controls. They did not replicate exactly.

questions.q: The ERA 'deprivation-specific' pattern includes:
questions.why: The ERA deprivation-specific pattern includes quasi-autism and disinhibited social engagement (Rutter, Sonuga-Barke). It does not include better attachment or enhanced IQ.

questions.q: Orben & Przybylski (2019) estimated digital technology use explained about what share of variance in adolescent wellbeing (upper bound)?
questions.why: Orben and Przybylski (2019) estimated digital technology use explained at most about 0.4% of the variance in adolescent wellbeing, a very small share.

questions.q: Why is using disorganised attachment classifications in child-protection decisions criticised?
options: They're not diagnostic of maltreatment for individuals
questions.why: Disorganised attachment classifications are criticised for child-protection decisions because they are not diagnostic of maltreatment for individuals (Granqvist et al., 2017).

questions.q: The 'transmission gap' implies researchers should examine mechanisms beyond sensitivity, such as:
questions.why: Given the transmission gap, researchers should look beyond sensitivity to mechanisms such as mentalisation or reflective functioning and contextual factors (Fonagy, Meins). IQ, genetics alone or birth order do not fill it.

courses.title: Cognition, Memory, Emotion and Decision Science
courses.summary: An advanced review of models of memory and attention, theories of emotion from basic-emotion to constructionist accounts, and judgement and decision-making from heuristics-and-biases to ecological rationality — with replication status marked.
outcomes: Learners can compare multi-store, working-memory, systems and consolidation/reconsolidation models with key evidence
Learners can evaluate models of attention and executive function and the ego-depletion controversy
Learners can contrast basic-emotion, appraisal and constructionist theories and the facial-expression evidence
Learners can critically assess heuristics-and-biases, dual-process and ecological-rationality programmes
Learners can state the replication status of prominent findings (facial feedback, ego depletion, hot hand, nudges)

scenes.text: In 2000, Nader, Schafe and LeDoux reported that a consolidated fear memory in rats became sensitive to a protein-synthesis inhibitor when it was reactivated.
Retrieval seemed to make the memory labile again — 'reconsolidation'.
Dr. Sameer Joshi, a clinical psychologist in Mumbai, wonders whether this could help PTSD patients.
He discovers both promise and a long list of boundary conditions and replication issues.

steps.title: Architectures
steps.body:
- **Modal model** (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968): sensory → STM → LTM with control processes.
- **Working memory** (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; Baddeley, 2000): central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer. Capacity limits: ~4 chunks (Cowan, 2001) rather than Miller's 7 ± 2.
- **Embedded-processes** model (Cowan): working memory as the activated portion of LTM with a focus of attention.
- **Memory systems** (Squire; Tulving): declarative (episodic, semantic) vs nondeclarative (procedural, priming, conditioning). Tulving's (1972) episodic–semantic distinction; **encoding specificity** (Tulving & Thomson, 1973); **transfer-appropriate processing** (Morris, Bransford & Franks, 1977) refines levels of processing (Craik & Lockhart, 1972).

steps.title: Consolidation and reconsolidation
steps.body:
- **Standard consolidation theory:** the hippocampus is temporarily needed; memories become neocortically independent over time (temporally graded retrograde amnesia).
- **Multiple trace theory / trace transformation** (Nadel & Moscovitch, 1997; Winocur & Moscovitch): detailed episodic memories remain hippocampus-dependent; semanticised versions become cortical.
- **Complementary learning systems** (McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly, 1995): fast hippocampal learning + slow cortical learning avoids catastrophic interference; sleep-related replay supports consolidation.
- **Reconsolidation** (Nader et al., 2000): reactivated memories may become labile and require restabilisation. Human applications (e.g., propranolol after reactivation; Kindt et al., 2009) show **mixed replication** and boundary conditions (memory age, strength, prediction error needed to destabilise).

steps.title: Reconstruction and false memory
steps.body:
- **DRM paradigm** (Roediger & McDermott, 1995; after Deese, 1959): studying *bed, rest, dream…* produces high-confidence false recall of *sleep*.
- **Misinformation effect** (Loftus & Palmer, 1974; Loftus, 2005 review).
- **Source-monitoring framework** (Johnson, Hashtroudi & Lindsay, 1993): false memories as source attribution errors.
- **Rich false memories** ('lost in the mall', Loftus & Pickrell, 1995): a minority of participants develop full or partial false memories; a 2017 mega-analysis of implantation studies (Scoboria et al.) estimated around 30% formed false memories, with substantial variation by coding criteria.
- Schacter's 'seven sins of memory' (transience, absent-mindedness, blocking, misattribution, suggestibility, bias, persistence) frames errors as by-products of adaptive design.

steps.title: Learning science with strong evidence
steps.body:
- **Testing effect** (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006): retrieval practice outperformed restudy at delays (repeated testing led to much better recall after a week despite lower confidence).
- **Spacing effect** (Cepeda et al., 2006 meta-analysis): optimal gap scales with the retention interval.
- **Interleaving** benefits category learning and maths problem selection (Rohrer & Taylor).
- **Desirable difficulties** (Bjork): conditions that slow acquisition can improve retention and transfer.
- 'Learning styles' matching (visual/auditory/kinaesthetic) lacks support (Pashler et al., 2008).

steps.title: Contested points
steps.body:
- Whether hippocampal involvement in remote memory is time-limited (SCT) or persistent for detailed episodes (MTT) — still debated.
- Translational reconsolidation therapies are not established clinical practice.
- The 'repressed memory' debate ('memory wars'): clinicians and memory researchers continue to disagree about dissociative amnesia; suggestive recovery techniques can create false memories.

options: Encoding processes match those required at retrieval
quiz.why: Transfer-appropriate processing says memory is best when encoding processes match those required at retrieval (Morris et al., 1977). Depth alone does not guarantee good retrieval.

quiz.why: Complementary learning systems explain slow cortical learning as a way to avoid catastrophic interference, where new learning overwrites old, as shown in network learning theory.

quiz.why: Human reconsolidation-blockade findings are mixed, with boundary conditions. They are not universally replicated or a clinical standard.

quiz.why: Pashler et al. (2008) concluded that matching instruction to 'learning styles' lacks adequate evidence, since the meshing hypothesis is unsupported.

lessons.title: Attention, executive function and the ego-depletion controversy

scenes.text: In 1998, Baumeister and colleagues reported that people who resisted cookies (eating radishes instead) gave up sooner on unsolvable puzzles — 'ego depletion'.
Hundreds of studies followed; a 2010 meta-analysis estimated a medium effect.
In 2016, a Registered Replication Report across 23 labs found an effect close to zero.
Prof. Hana Suzuki, reviewing for a journal, now asks every self-control paper for preregistration and power.

steps.title: Models of attention
steps.body:
- **Early vs late selection** (Broadbent, 1958; Deutsch & Deutsch; Treisman's attenuation).
- **Load theory** (Lavie): perceptual load determines distractor processing; cognitive load can increase it.
- **Spatial cueing** (Posner, 1980): costs and benefits of valid/invalid cues; endogenous vs exogenous orienting; inhibition of return.
- **Feature integration theory** (Treisman & Gelade, 1980): features registered in parallel; attention binds conjunctions (serial search slopes) — later modified by Guided Search (Wolfe).
- **Biased competition** (Desimone & Duncan, 1995): objects compete for neural representation; top-down signals bias competition.
- Attention networks (Posner & Petersen): alerting, orienting, executive control.

steps.title: Executive functions
steps.body:
**Miyake et al. (2000):** latent-variable analysis showed 'unity and diversity' — inhibition, shifting and updating are correlated but separable. Later work (Friedman & Miyake, 2017) suggests a common EF factor with shifting- and updating-specific factors (inhibition largely absorbed into common EF).

Behavioural self-control tasks (Stroop, stop-signal) and self-report self-control correlate weakly — the 'reliability paradox' (Hedge, Powell & Sumner, 2018): robust experimental effects often have poor between-person reliability, limiting individual-differences research.

steps.title: Ego depletion: a case study
steps.body:
- **Original:** Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven & Tice (1998); strength model of self-control.
- **Meta-analysis:** Hagger et al. (2010), d ≈ 0.62. Carter & McCullough (2014) found strong evidence of small-study effects/publication bias; bias-corrected estimates near zero.
- **Glucose hypothesis:** later challenged (e.g., Kurzban; failed replications; Vadillo et al., 2016).
- **RRR:** Hagger et al. (2016), 23 labs, N ≈ 2,100, sequential-task paradigm: d ≈ 0.04, CI including zero.
- **Follow-ups:** a further multi-site test (Vohs et al., 2021, 36 labs) found an effect near zero (d ≈ 0.06 in their primary analysis).
- **Status:** the robust, general depletion effect is not supported as originally conceived; alternative accounts emphasise motivation and attention shifts (Inzlicht & Schmeichel, 2012).

steps.title: Lessons for evaluating a literature
steps.body:
- A large number of significant studies ≠ a real effect when designs are small and flexible.
- Meta-analyses inherit publication bias; use bias-sensitive methods (PET-PEESE, selection models, z-curve) and compare with preregistered multi-lab tests.
- Manipulation checks and task heterogeneity matter: the RRR used one standardised paradigm, which critics argued was weak — an example of how 'failed replications' are themselves debated.

quiz.why: Miyake et al. (2000) identified inhibition, shifting and updating as the three executive functions, under unity and diversity.

quiz.why: The reliability paradox (Hedge et al., 2018) says robust experimental effects often have poor between-person reliability, because they have low between-subject variance.

quiz.why: The 2016 ego-depletion registered replication report (Hagger et al.) found an effect near zero, about d = 0.04.

lessons.title: Theories of emotion and the facial-expression debate

scenes.text: In 1988, Strack, Martin and Stepper reported that holding a pen in the teeth (forcing a smile-like expression) made cartoons seem funnier than holding it in the lips.
In 2016, a 17-lab Registered Replication Report found no effect.

Critics noted the replication filmed participants, which might change the effect. A 2018 study without cameras found an effect; a later large collaboration found effects for some poses but not the pen procedure.
Prof. Daniel Okoye prepares a lecture: 'What the facial feedback saga teaches about emotion — and science.'

steps.title: Three families of theory
steps.body:
1. **Basic emotion theories** (Tomkins; Ekman; Izard; Panksepp's subcortical systems): a small set of evolved emotions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, disgust, surprise ± contempt) with distinctive signals and physiology.
2. **Appraisal theories** (Arnold; Lazarus; Scherer's component process model; Frijda): emotions arise from evaluations of events' relevance to goals (novelty, valence, goal congruence, coping potential, norm compatibility). Lazarus–Zajonc debate (1980s) on whether affect requires cognition.
3. **Psychological constructionism** (Russell's **core affect** — valence × arousal circumplex, 1980/2003; Barrett's **theory of constructed emotion**, 2017): emotions are constructed from core affect plus conceptual knowledge and context; categories lack consistent biological 'fingerprints'.

Plus revived **James–Lange** ideas and **interoception** research (Craig; Garfinkel).

steps.title: Universality of facial expressions
steps.body:
- **Pro-universality:** Ekman & Friesen (1971), the Fore of Papua New Guinea matched faces to stories at above-chance rates; meta-analyses of recognition (Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002) find above-chance recognition with an **in-group advantage**.
- **Challenges:** recognition rates drop with free-labelling instead of forced choice; studies with the Himba (Gendron et al., 2014) and Trobrianders (Crivelli et al., 2016) found weaker or different patterns.
- **Barrett et al. (2019)** review (*Psychological Science in the Public Interest*): people do not reliably produce or infer specific emotions from facial configurations across contexts with the consistency assumed — 'emotion recognition' technologies are not well supported.

**Status: contested.** Many researchers accept above-chance recognition for prototypical posed expressions but dispute that faces reliably reveal internal states in everyday life.

steps.title: Facial feedback: replication case
steps.body:
- Strack et al. (1988) pen paradigm.
- **Wagenmakers et al. (2016) RRR**, 17 labs: no evidence of effect.
- Noah, Schul & Mayo (2018): observation (cameras) may eliminate the effect.
- **Coles, Larsen & Lench (2019)** meta-analysis (286 effects): small overall effect, with heterogeneity and possible bias.
- **Many Smiles Collaboration** (Coles et al., 2022, *Nature Human Behaviour*; 19 countries): voluntary smiling and facial mimicry increased self-reported happiness modestly; the pen-in-mouth task did not produce a reliable effect.

**Current reading:** small facial feedback effects on self-reported feelings likely exist under some conditions; strong claims are unwarranted.

steps.title: Emotion regulation and the somatic marker hypothesis
steps.body:
- **Gross's process model** (1998, 2015): situation selection/modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change (reappraisal), response modulation. Reappraisal is generally linked to better outcomes than habitual suppression, but effectiveness depends on context (regulatory flexibility; Bonanno & Burton, 2013).
- **Somatic marker hypothesis** (Damasio; Bechara et al., 1994, Iowa Gambling Task): bodily signals guide decisions. Critiques (Maia & McClelland, 2004; Dunn, Dalgleish & Lawrence, 2006): participants may have explicit knowledge of deck contingencies; the IGT confounds several processes.

steps.title: What to teach as settled vs open
steps.body:
- Settled-ish: emotions involve coordinated changes in appraisal, physiology, expression and experience; valence and arousal capture much variance in self-reported affect; reappraisal tends to beat suppression on average.
- Open: whether discrete emotions are natural kinds; the degree of universality of expression; facial feedback magnitude; mechanisms of interoception's role.

lessons.title: Judgement and decision-making: biases, heuristics and ecological rationality

story.title: The hot hand that came back

scenes.text: In 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky concluded that basketball's 'hot hand' was a cognitive illusion.
In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo showed the original analysis contained a subtle selection bias; correcting it revealed evidence of a modest hot hand.
Prof. Leela Raman teaches decision science in Ahmedabad. She uses the story to show how even classic 'biases' can be revisited.
Decision science is a field of strong findings — and strong debates.

steps.title: Normative, descriptive, prescriptive
steps.body:
- **Normative** models: expected utility (von Neumann–Morgenstern), Bayesian updating, logic.
- **Descriptive:** what people do — **prospect theory** (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; cumulative version 1992): reference dependence, loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity, probability weighting.
- **Prescriptive:** how to help — decision aids, debiasing, choice architecture.

Ruggeri et al. (2020, *Nature Human Behaviour*) replicated core prospect-theory items across 19 countries (~4,000 participants) with high rates of replication. Loss aversion's magnitude and generality are **debated**: Gal & Rucker (2018) argue many 'loss aversion' effects reflect other mechanisms; others defend it (e.g., Mrkva et al., 2020).

steps.title: Heuristics-and-biases vs ecological rationality
steps.body:
- **Heuristics and biases** (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974): representativeness, availability, anchoring produce systematic errors relative to normative standards; conjunction fallacy (the 'Linda problem', 1983); base-rate neglect.
- **Ecological rationality** (Gigerenzer; Todd & Gigerenzer): heuristics like **recognition** and **take-the-best** can be accurate in the right environments ('less-is-more'); **natural frequency** formats dramatically improve Bayesian reasoning (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995).
- The debate (Kahneman & Tversky, 1996 vs Gigerenzer, 1996) is partly about which norms apply and how problems are represented.

steps.title: Dual-process theories
steps.body:
Type 1 (fast, autonomous) vs Type 2 (slow, working-memory dependent) processing (Evans & Stanovich, 2013); Kahneman's System 1/System 2 popularisation.
- Supporting evidence: cognitive reflection test (Frederick, 2005), belief bias, effects of time pressure and load.
- Critiques: unclear criteria for type membership; intuitions can be logical (De Neys's 'logical intuitions'); single-process alternatives (Kruglanski & Gigerenzer, 2011; Keren & Schul, 2009).
- **Default-interventionist vs parallel** architectures remain debated.

steps.title: Applied decision science and replication
steps.body:
- **Nudges:** Mertens et al. (2022, *PNAS*) meta-analysis reported d ≈ 0.43 overall; Maier et al. (2022, *PNAS* letter) found that after correcting for publication bias there was little evidence for an overall effect, though some categories (e.g., defaults) may be robust. DellaVigna & Linos (2022) found nudge-unit RCT effects (≈ 1.4 percentage points) far smaller than in academic papers.
- **Anchoring** replicates robustly in many paradigms (Many Labs 1).
- **Hot hand:** Miller & Sanjurjo (2018) — finite-sample selection bias in streak analyses.
- **Choice overload** ('jam study', Iyengar & Lepper, 2000): meta-analysis (Scheibehenne et al., 2010) found mean effect near zero with high heterogeneity; later work identifies moderators (Chernev et al., 2015).
- **Wisdom of crowds**, **superforecasting** (Tetlock & Gardner): calibration and aggregation improve forecasts.

steps.title: Teaching with honesty
steps.body: Tell students which findings are robust (anchoring, framing in many contexts, base-rate neglect with probability formats, defaults), which are contested (loss-aversion generality, ego depletion, choice overload, many priming effects), and which were reversed (strong 'no hot hand' claim). The field's self-correction is itself a lesson in rationality.

courses.title: Social Influence and Personality Science Revisited
courses.summary: An expert re-reading of social psychology's classic influence studies, the social-priming and implicit-bias controversies, the structure and development of personality, and dimensional models of personality pathology.
outcomes: Learners can re-interpret Asch, Milgram and the 1971 prison simulation in light of archival and replication work

scenes.text: Psychologist-historian Dr. Ellen Varghese spends a sabbatical reading accounts of Milgram's obedience archives and recent reanalyses.
She finds procedures varied more than textbooks suggest, and many participants doubted the shocks were real.
Yet the core variations — proximity, authority's presence, peer rebellion — remain informative.
Her new lecture: 'What these studies really show, and what they don't.'

steps.title: Asch and conformity
steps.body:
Asch (1951, 1956): errors on about a third of critical trials; ~75% conformed at least once; one dissenter cut conformity sharply.

**Bond & Smith (1996)** meta-analysis of 133 line-judgement studies across 17 countries: conformity declined in the US since the 1950s and was higher in collectivist cultures.

**Moscovici** (1969, 'blue–green' slides): a **consistent minority** can shift majority judgements (minority influence, often via private/indirect change — conversion theory).

steps.title: Milgram reinterpreted
steps.body:
- Baseline (Milgram, 1963): 26/40 (65%) to 450 V; obedience fell when the experimenter was absent, the learner was close, or peers refused (as low as ~10% with two rebelling peers).
- **Gina Perry (2012)** and others: deviations from standardised prods, debriefing problems, and many participants' scepticism about the shocks.
- **Haslam, Reicher and colleagues:** 'engaged followership' — participants continued when they identified with the scientific enterprise, not from blind obedience; the prod 'You have no other choice, you must go on' tended to produce *refusal* (Haslam, Reicher & Birney, 2014).
- **Burger (2009)** partial replication to 150 V; Polish replication (Doliński et al., 2017) found high obedience rates.

**Status:** high obedience under these conditions is robust; the 'agentic state' explanation is contested.

steps.title: The 1971 prison simulation and the BBC Prison Study
steps.body:
Zimbardo's 1971 prison simulation is widely taught as showing that roles quickly corrupt. **Archival critiques** (Le Texier, 2018/2019): guards were instructed and encouraged towards harshness; demand characteristics were strong; it was not a controlled experiment.

The **BBC Prison Study** (Reicher & Haslam, 2002/2006) found that guards did not automatically become tyrannical; group identification and leadership shaped outcomes. Teach the 1971 study as a demonstration with severe methodological and ethical problems.

steps.title: Helping and the bystander effect
steps.body:
- Darley & Latané (1968): diffusion of responsibility.
- **Fischer et al. (2011)** meta-analysis (>50 years, ~7,700 participants): bystander effect present overall but **attenuated in dangerous emergencies**, when perpetrators are present, and when bystanders can help physically.
- **Philpot et al. (2020, *American Psychologist*)**: CCTV of real public conflicts in the UK, Netherlands and South Africa — at least one bystander intervened in about 90% of incidents; more bystanders → greater likelihood someone helps.
- Darley & Batson (1973) 'Good Samaritan': time pressure reduced helping more than personality/religiosity measures.

steps.title: Teaching responsibly
steps.body: Present classic studies with their **methods, archival critiques and replications**, distinguishing robust phenomena (conformity pressures, situational variation in obedience) from contested explanations and from discredited narratives (Kitty Genovese's '38 witnesses').

lessons.title: Social cognition under scrutiny: priming, stereotype threat, implicit bias

scenes.text: In 1996, Bargh, Chen and Burrows reported that students primed with elderly-related words walked more slowly down a corridor.
In 2012, Doyen and colleagues used infrared timing and found no effect — unless experimenters expected one.
Daniel Kahneman wrote an open letter calling priming research a 'train wreck looming' and urging replication.
Dr. Ritu Banerjee, editing a textbook in Kolkata, must decide which findings stay in.

steps.title: Behavioural/social priming
steps.body:
- **Elderly priming** (Bargh et al., 1996) → Doyen et al. (2012): no effect with automated timing; effect appeared when experimenters held expectations.
- **Money priming**, professor priming ('intelligence' primes; Dijksterhuis & van Knippenberg, 1998) → large multi-lab replication failures (e.g., O'Donnell et al., 2018 RRR on professor priming: no effect).
- Many Labs projects found several social-priming effects did not replicate.

Distinguish **semantic/repetition priming** in cognitive psychology (robust; e.g., lexical decision facilitation) from **behavioural priming** claims (weak replication record).

steps.title: Stereotype threat
steps.body:
Steele & Aronson (1995): Black students performed worse on a verbal test framed as diagnostic of ability. Hundreds of studies followed.
- **Flore & Wicherts (2015)** meta-analysis on girls' maths performance: small average effect with signs of publication bias.
- **Flore, Mulder & Wicherts (2018)**: large preregistered study in Dutch high schools found no effect.
- **Shewach et al. (2019)** in high-stakes testing contexts found small effects.

**Status:** contested; effects in real-world testing are likely small and context-dependent. Social-belonging and values-affirmation interventions show mixed but sometimes promising results in large trials.

steps.title: Implicit bias and the IAT
steps.body:
- **IAT** (Greenwald, McGhee & Schwartz, 1998) measures association strength by reaction-time differences.
- **Reliability:** test–retest roughly r ≈ 0.4–0.5 — too low for individual diagnosis.
- **Predictive validity:** Greenwald et al. (2009) reported modest correlations with behaviour; **Oswald et al. (2013)** found IAT scores predicted discrimination poorly and no better than explicit measures.
- **Forscher et al. (2019)** meta-analysis: implicit measures can be changed, but changes don't reliably produce changes in explicit measures or behaviour.
- Population-level IAT averages may track regional disparities (Payne, Vuletich & Lundberg's 'bias of crowds').

Implications: unconscious-bias trainings built on single IAT scores have weak evidence for changing behaviour; structural interventions (structured interviews, blind review, accountability) have better support.

steps.title: How to decide what stays in a textbook
steps.body: Ask of each finding: original sample size and design; independent preregistered replications; bias-corrected meta-analyses; mechanism plausibility; real-world effect size. Keep historically important studies but present them with their replication status. Prejudice and discrimination are real and well documented by **audit studies** (e.g., Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004; caste-related audit studies in India such as Thorat & Attewell, 2007) — the debate is about specific measures and mechanisms.

scenes.text: Prof. Javed Akhtar in Lucknow analyses 20 years of personality data from a cohort study.
Rank-order stability is high in midlife, yet average conscientiousness rose and neuroticism fell across adulthood.
Conscientiousness predicted job performance and health behaviours; effects were modest but persistent.
Personality is stable *and* changing — the key is which kind of stability.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Big Five / Five-Factor Model** (lexical tradition: Goldberg; questionnaire tradition: Costa & McCrae's NEO-PI-R): Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Openness. Each has facets (e.g., NEO's 6 per domain; BFI-2's 3 per domain; DeYoung's two 'aspects' per domain).
- **HEXACO** (Ashton & Lee): adds **Honesty–Humility**; re-arranges agreeableness and emotionality. Honesty–Humility predicts unethical behaviour and the 'dark triad' overlap.
- Higher-order 'metatraits' (stability, plasticity) and a 'general factor of personality' are contested (often attributed to response style/social desirability).
- Cross-cultural replicability of the five factors is good in WEIRD and many other samples but weaker in some low-literacy, non-Western samples (e.g., Gurven et al., 2013, Tsimane).

steps.title: Heritability and genetics
steps.body:
- Twin studies: heritability around **40%** for Big Five traits (Vukasović & Bratko, 2015 meta-analysis), with little shared-environment variance; the rest is non-shared environment and measurement error.
- Polderman et al. (2015) twin meta-analysis across all human traits found an average heritability around 49%.
- **GWAS:** many variants each of tiny effect; SNP-based heritability lower than twin estimates ('missing heritability').

steps.title: Stability and change
steps.body:
- **Rank-order stability** rises with age, plateauing around r ≈ 0.7 in later adulthood (Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000).
- **Mean-level change** (Roberts, Walton & Viechtbauer, 2006): increases in conscientiousness, agreeableness and emotional stability across adulthood — the **maturity principle**; social investment theory links change to adult roles (work, partnering).
- **Intervention:** Roberts et al. (2017) systematic review: personality traits (especially neuroticism) changed with clinical interventions, with an average effect around d ≈ 0.37 over ~24 weeks.
- **Volitional change** studies (Hudson & Fraley) show people can change traits they want to change, modestly.

steps.title: Predictive validity
steps.body:
**Roberts et al. (2007), 'The power of personality':** traits predicted mortality, divorce and occupational attainment with effect sizes comparable to socioeconomic status and cognitive ability.
- Conscientiousness: job performance (meta-analytic ρ ≈ 0.2–0.3, Barrick & Mount and later), health behaviours, longevity (Friedman's Terman follow-up).
- Neuroticism: strong predictor of internalising disorders and public-health costs (Lahey, 2009).
- Effects per individual are modest; aggregated across many decisions and years they matter.

steps.title: Contested points
steps.body:
- **Person–situation debate** (Mischel, 1968, 'personality coefficient' ~0.30) resolved largely by aggregation (Epstein) and person × situation interaction (Mischel & Shoda's CAPS; Fleeson's whole-trait theory: traits as density distributions of states).
- **Type indicators:** many popular type-based tools show poor test–retest stability of categories and are not recommended for selection.
- Self-report biases and reference-group effects complicate cross-cultural mean comparisons.

scenes.text: A psychiatrist in Delhi, Dr. Nalini Rao, assesses a patient who meets criteria for three different DSM personality disorders — and none perfectly.
She tries the ICD-11 approach: rate overall severity, then trait domains.
The description becomes clearer and more useful for treatment planning.
Dimensional models are reshaping how clinicians and researchers think about personality pathology.

steps.title: Problems with categorical personality disorders
steps.body: DSM's ten categorical PDs (Clusters A, B, C) suffer from high comorbidity, arbitrary thresholds, within-category heterogeneity (e.g., there are many combinations of 5 out of 9 criteria for borderline PD), poor stability of categories, and frequent use of 'PD not otherwise specified'.

steps.title: DSM-5 Section III and ICD-11
steps.body:
- **DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD),** Section III: **Criterion A** — level of personality functioning (self: identity, self-direction; interpersonal: empathy, intimacy); **Criterion B** — 25 pathological trait facets in five domains (Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, Psychoticism), measured by the PID-5. The categorical model remains in Section II.
- **ICD-11** (in effect 2022): personality disorder graded by **severity** (mild, moderate, severe) plus optional **trait domain qualifiers**: negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia; and a **borderline pattern** specifier (retained after debate).

steps.title: HiTOP and the p-factor
steps.body:
- **HiTOP** (Kotov et al., 2017): a hierarchical, empirically derived taxonomy — symptoms → syndromes → subfactors → spectra (internalising, thought disorder, disinhibited externalising, antagonistic externalising, detachment, somatoform) → superspectra.
- **p-factor** (Caspi et al., 2014, Dunedin): a general psychopathology factor captures shared liability across disorders. Interpretation is debated (statistical artefact vs meaningful construct like impulsive responsivity to emotion or thought disorder).
- PD trait domains map closely onto Big Five extremes (negative affectivity ↔ neuroticism; detachment ↔ low extraversion; antagonism ↔ low agreeableness; disinhibition ↔ low conscientiousness; psychoticism ↔ partly openness-related).

steps.title: Treatment evidence
steps.body: For borderline PD, structured psychotherapies have the best evidence: **DBT** (Linehan), **mentalisation-based treatment** (Bateman & Fonagy), **schema therapy**, **transference-focused psychotherapy**; general psychiatric management (Gunderson) performs comparably to DBT in some trials. Medication is not a primary treatment for BPD (NICE guidance). Prognosis is better than once believed: in the McLean Study of Adult Development, most patients achieved symptomatic remission over the follow-up years, though functional recovery lagged.

steps.title: Contested points
steps.body:
- Whether to keep named PD categories (clinical communication) or move fully dimensional.
- The meaning of the p-factor.
- Cultural validity of PD constructs and trait norms, including in Indian clinical populations.

*Clinical content here is for professional education, not individual diagnosis.*

courses.title: The Replication Crisis and Current Debates in Psychology
courses.summary: What happened when psychology tested itself: the large replication projects, the statistical and incentive causes, the reforms now reshaping the field, the measurement and generalisability critiques, and live debates (growth mindset, power posing, positivity ratios, and more).
outcomes: Learners can summarise the major replication projects with their key numbers
Learners can explain how low power, flexibility, publication bias and incentives combine to produce false findings
Learners can evaluate reforms: preregistration, Registered Reports, multi-site studies, open data, bias-corrected meta-analysis
Learners can apply measurement and generalisability critiques (WEIRD samples, constraints on generality)
Learners can present balanced accounts of contested findings in current teaching and practice

scenes.text: In 2011, a top journal published Daryl Bem's experiments claiming evidence that people could 'feel the future'.
The same year, Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn showed that flexible analyses could 'prove' that listening to a Beatles song made people younger.
Also in 2011, investigations revealed that a prominent Dutch social psychologist, Diederik Stapel, had fabricated data.
Prof. Anand Kulkarni, chairing a department in Pune, decides his graduate methods course must change.

steps.title: The big projects and their numbers
steps.body:
- **Open Science Collaboration (2015, *Science*)** — Reproducibility Project: Psychology: 100 replications of studies from three 2008 journals. 97% of originals reported significant results; **36%** of replications did. Replication effect sizes were on average about **half** the original.
- **Many Labs 1** (Klein et al., 2014): 13 effects across 36 samples; 10 replicated consistently, priming effects did not.
- **Many Labs 2** (Klein et al., 2018): 28 classic and contemporary findings across ~125 samples in many countries; about **half** (14) replicated; heterogeneity across samples was generally small.
- **Social Sciences Replication Project** (Camerer et al., 2018, *Nature Human Behaviour*): 21 experiments from *Nature* and *Science* (2010–2015); **13** replicated; effect sizes about half.
- **Registered Replication Reports** (*Perspectives on Psychological Science*/AMPPS): ego depletion, facial feedback, professor priming — near-zero effects; verbal overshadowing — replicated (smaller than original).

steps.title: Why Bem (2011) mattered
steps.body: Bem's nine experiments used standard methods of the time and reported mostly significant results for precognition. Most scientists considered the conclusion implausible — so the paper forced the question: *if standard practices can produce this, what else have they produced?* Wagenmakers et al. (2011) re-analysed with Bayesian methods; preregistered replications (e.g., Galak et al., 2012) found no effect.

steps.title: Interpreting 'replication failure'
steps.body: A failed replication does not prove an original was false; possible reasons include original false positive, inflated original estimate, low replication power, hidden moderators, or procedural differences. Debates followed the OSC project (Gilbert, King, Pettigrew & Wilson, 2016 critique; Anderson et al., 2016 reply). Most methodologists conclude the evidence indicates substantial inflation and false positives in the published record, varying by subfield.

steps.title: Why many published findings may be false
steps.body:
Ioannidis (2005) model: positive predictive value (PPV) = (1 − β)R / ((1 − β)R + α), with R = prior odds a tested hypothesis is true.
- If R = 0.25 (1 in 5 hypotheses true), power = 0.35, α = 0.05: PPV = (0.35 × 0.25) / (0.0875 + 0.05) ≈ **0.64**.
- Add bias/flexibility and PPV drops further.

With power 0.8 instead: PPV = 0.2/(0.2 + 0.05) = 0.80. Power and prior plausibility matter as much as α.

steps.title: Balanced perspective
steps.body: Replication rates differ across subfields (cognitive effects tended to replicate more often than social effects in OSC 2015) and are not unique to psychology — similar projects in cancer biology (Errington et al., 2021) and economics experiments found related problems. The crisis has also produced one of science's most vigorous reform movements.

quiz.why: Camerer et al. (2018) replicated 13 of 21 Nature/Science social science experiments.

quiz.why: Many Labs 2 found heterogeneity across samples was generally small: effects either replicated broadly or not.

quiz.why: Ioannidis's positive predictive value rises with higher power and higher prior odds. Low power, small samples and more flexibility lower it.

lessons.title: Why it happened: statistics and incentives

scenes.text: PhD scholar Shalini in Hyderabad notices her lab's habits: run 20 participants, peek, add 10 more if 'close'; drop the condition that 'didn't work'.
Only 'clean' significant results get written up; the rest go into a folder called 'pilot'.
Hiring and promotion count first-author papers in high-impact journals.
No one is a villain. The system rewards exactly what produces unreliable findings.

steps.title: Statistical ingredients
steps.body:
- **Low power:** Cohen (1962) found low median power in psychology; Button et al. (2013) found median power ~21% in the neuroscience studies they examined; Szucs & Ioannidis (2017) found low power in cognitive neuroscience and psychology.
- **Researcher degrees of freedom** (Simmons et al., 2011): optional stopping, flexible exclusions, covariates, DVs, conditions.
- **Garden of forking paths** (Gelman & Loken): data-contingent choices without conscious fishing.
- **HARKing** (Kerr, 1998).
- **Publication bias / file drawer** (Rosenthal, 1979): positive-result rate in psychology was among the highest of sciences (Fanelli, 2010).
- **Misinterpretation of p-values** and dichotomous thinking (ASA statement, 2016).

steps.title: Incentive ingredients
steps.body:
- 'Publish or perish', novelty preference, and journals' preference for clean narratives
- Smaldino & McElreath (2016), 'The natural selection of bad science': agent-based model showing labs using low-power, high-output methods 'outcompete' careful labs under productivity incentives — and that replication alone doesn't fix it
- Survey evidence of QRPs (John, Loewenstein & Prelec, 2012; later surveys with different wording found lower but still non-trivial rates, e.g., Fiedler & Schwarz, 2016)
- Rare but impactful fraud (Stapel; others) — distinct from QRPs, but enabled by lack of data sharing

steps.title: Detecting bias in a literature
steps.body:
Tools for bias-sensitive synthesis:
- **Funnel plots** and **Egger's test** (small-study effects)
- **PET-PEESE** (precision-effect test/estimate with standard error)
- **Selection models** (e.g., three-parameter selection model)
- **p-curve** (Simonsohn, Nelson & Simmons, 2014): distribution of significant p-values; right skew suggests evidential value
- **z-curve** (Brunner & Schimmack; Bartoš & Schimmack): estimates expected replication and discovery rates
- **Robust Bayesian meta-analysis** (RoBMA; Maier, Bartoš & Wagenmakers)

No method is perfect under high heterogeneity; triangulate with preregistered multi-lab studies.

steps.title: Contested points
steps.body:
- How prevalent QRPs really are (survey wording matters).
- Whether hidden moderators explain many failures (most multi-lab data suggest heterogeneity is smaller than often assumed).
- Whether α = 0.005 should replace 0.05 for new discoveries (Benjamin et al., 2018) vs 'justify your alpha' (Lakens et al., 2018).
