lessons.title: Reforms: what changed and what works

story.title: A Registered Report in her first year

scenes.text: Ayesha, a first-year PhD scholar in Delhi, submits a Registered Report: introduction, methods and analysis plan — no data yet.
Reviewers improve her design; the journal grants in-principle acceptance.
Her result turns out null. The paper is published anyway — and cited by a meta-analysis a year later.
The reforms are changing what a successful early career looks like.

steps.title: Preregistration and Registered Reports
steps.body:
- **Preregistration** (OSF, AsPredicted): reduces undisclosed flexibility; deviations must be reported. Studies of preregistrations show they are often vague and deviations under-reported (e.g., Claesen et al., 2021) — quality matters.
- **Registered Reports** (Chambers; *Cortex* 2013; now offered by hundreds of journals): Stage 1 peer review before data collection, in-principle acceptance. Scheel et al. (2021): ~44% positive results vs ~96% in standard reports. Soderberg et al. (2021): Registered Reports rated as equal or higher on rigour and quality by blind reviewers.

steps.title: Big-team and open science
steps.body:
- **Multi-site collaborations:** Many Labs, **Psychological Science Accelerator** (a global network of labs; e.g., Jones et al., 2021 face-perception study across 41 countries), Many Babies (infant research), Many Smiles
- **Open data, materials and code**; badges (Kidwell et al., 2016, showed badges at *Psychological Science* increased data sharing)
- **TOP guidelines** (Nosek et al., 2015) for journal transparency
- **Preprints** (PsyArXiv) and post-publication review
- **Adversarial collaborations** (Kahneman's proposal; e.g., theories of consciousness tested by Cogitate consortium)

steps.title: Better statistics and inference
steps.body:
- Effect sizes and CIs; **SESOI** and equivalence tests
- **Sequential designs** with planned interim analyses (controlling α)
- **Bayesian** estimation and Bayes factors
- Multiverse/specification-curve analyses
- Simulation-based power for complex designs
- **Constraints on generality** statements (Simons, Shoda & Lindsay, 2017)

steps.title: Assessing a reform's success
steps.body:
Evidence that reforms help:
- Large preregistered multi-lab projects now give direct, less biased effect estimates instead of relying on a selectively published literature.
- Rising sample sizes in major journals; increasing data sharing.

Open questions: replication of reform effects across subfields, burden on early-career and Global South researchers, and how to fund replications.

steps.title: Equity in reform
steps.body: Big-team science and open data can deepen inequities if they assume high-bandwidth infrastructure and English-language publishing. Inclusion of Global South labs (including Indian institutions) as full partners — not just data collectors — is part of good reform. Data sharing must respect consent and privacy (e.g., India's DPDP Act 2023).

scenes.text: Prof. Rukmini Iyer revisits ten slides she has used for 20 years: power posing, growth mindset, the 2.9 positivity ratio, the marshmallow test, ego depletion, 'WEIRD' samples.
Some findings survived in smaller form, some reversed, some were never well supported.
She adds a 'status' badge to each slide: robust, contested, small, or unsupported.
Her students say it's the most memorable lecture of the year.

steps.title: WEIRD samples and generalisability
steps.body:
- **Arnett (2008):** 96% of samples in top psychology journals came from Western industrialised countries with ~12% of the world's population.
- **Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010):** WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic) people are often outliers (e.g., Müller-Lyer illusion susceptibility, fairness in economic games, analytic vs holistic cognition).
- **Yarkoni (2022), 'The generalizability crisis':** verbal hypotheses are tested with narrow operationalisations, and statistical models ignore variance from stimuli, settings and tasks, so inferences are overgeneralised.
- India-based research is a major opportunity: large, diverse populations; multilingual settings; but measurement invariance must be tested, not assumed.

steps.title: Measurement 'schmeasurement'
steps.body:
Flake & Fried (2020): questionable measurement practices — undefined constructs, ad hoc scales, unreported modifications, ignoring validity evidence — undermine conclusions even with perfect statistics. Flake, Pek & Hehman (2017) found validity evidence for scales in a top journal was often minimal (frequently only Cronbach's α).

**Jingle–jangle fallacies:** same name for different constructs (jingle); different names for the same construct (jangle) — e.g., grit's overlap with conscientiousness (Credé, Tynan & Harms, 2017).

steps.title: Status of famous findings (as of the mid-2020s)
steps.body:
- **Power posing** (Carney, Cuddy & Yap, 2010): hormonal effects failed to replicate (Ranehill et al., 2015); Carney (2016) publicly stated she no longer believed the effects were real; small effects on *self-reported feelings of power* may exist (debated). → **Hormonal/behavioural claims unsupported.**
- **Growth mindset interventions:** Sisk et al. (2018) meta-analyses found weak average effects (d ≈ 0.08), larger for low-SES/at-risk students; the National Study of Learning Mindsets (Yeager et al., 2019, *Nature*) found a small improvement in grades among lower-achieving students, with heterogeneity by school context. → **Small, context-dependent.**
- **Positivity ratio** (Fredrickson & Losada, 2005, '2.9013'): mathematical basis critiqued by Brown, Sokal & Friedman (2013); the modelling was formally withdrawn. → **Ratio unsupported** (positive emotions research continues).
- **Marshmallow test:** Watts et al. (2018) → associations smaller and largely explained by background. → **Small.**
- **Ego depletion:** multi-lab tests near zero. → **Unsupported as originally conceived.**
- **Bystander effect:** real but moderated; groups often help. → **Robust but nuanced.**
- **Anchoring, Stroop, testing effect, spacing effect:** → **Robust.**

steps.title: Other live debates
steps.body:
- Social media and adolescent mental health (see Course 1)
- Whether the p-factor is substantive
- Basic vs constructed emotions
- Implicit bias measurement
- Theory crisis: calls for formal modelling and stronger theory (e.g., Borsboom et al., 2021; Muthukrishna & Henrich, 2019)
- Psychedelic-assisted therapy trials: promising early results, with concerns about blinding and expectancy effects — status developing

steps.title: How experts should teach contested science
steps.body: Mark status explicitly; cite the strongest evidence on each side; distinguish phenomenon from explanation; avoid both credulity and cynicism. Remember that good science changes its mind — and say so to students.
